Activity sheet – Nationalism 
Summarising nationalism  
Summarising information makes it short, punchy and easy to understand. One way to 
summarise is to put information into short bullet points. 
The following paragraph describes nationalism. It looks like a huge chunk of information! 
Nationalism is a feeling of devotion towards your nation (country). Nationalism is a strong 
feeling – some people love their country so much they would even die in a war to defend 
it. Nationalism means people are willing to support the leaders of their country and make 
sacrifices. This devotion presents many advantages for the country’s leader. For example, they 
have more soldiers for their army, a workforce to make guns in their arms factories, more 
freedom to make unpopular decisions, greater national security and people more willing to 
make sacrifices such as rationing food. Leaders can use the symbols of a country to promote 
nationalism by emphasising how important their country is. This makes people feel more loyal 
towards their country. Examples of symbols include the national flag, colours and animals.  
At the time of World War I, nationalism was growing stronger in lots of countries, which meant 
people were willing to fight for, work for and defend their country against its enemies.

Defining imperialism 
Imperialism refers to the practice of taking over other countries. Countries do this to gain 
more power. Their enemies can see how much power they have and will be less likely to

Resource sheet – Imperialism 
How to build an empire 
The British Empire was a case study in how to build an empire. Over a number of years 
Britain had used its powerful navy to take over several other countries. By 1914 the British 
Empire ruled over a quarter of the land on Earth, despite being an island country. This 
gave Britain power all over the world, allowing it to influence other countries, control their 
decisions and use their resources to further expand the empire.
Britain claimed Australia’s land and people in 1770, making it part of the British Empire. 
Because it was such a large area, Australia was divided into smaller areas of land called 
colonies. This made it easier for Britain to control the land and the people. 
Even when the colonies were united under Federation and Australia became one single 
country it still remained under British control. Many Australians felt connected to the 
British Empire. They felt strong loyalty towards Britain, which they saw as the motherland, 
and would defend it in a fight. This is why Australia joined the fighting in World War I in 
order to defend the British Empire.

How to remember the causes of  
World War I 
In order to remember the four causes of World War I we use the acronym MAIN. An 
acronym is a word formed from the first letter of other words. 
• M – Militarism (military power)
• A – Alliances (friendships between countries)
• I – Imperialism (taking over other countries)
• N – Nationalism (loving your own country)
Another way to remember the four causes of World War I is to visualise them. 
+ 
1	 Draw a picture to represent each cause of World War I. 
Militarism
Imperialism
Alliances
Nationalism

Constructing essays
An essay is an effective way of demonstrating what you know about history. Essays are 
easier if you view them as a thing to be constructed, rather than written. One way to 
visualise this is to compare essay construction to house construction.
Just as a builder first meets with the land owners to find out what they want them 
to build, you need to first work out what an essay question is asking you to do. This is 
unpacking a question. One way to do this is to find synonyms for the key words used in 
the question. This allows you to explain the question in a different way.

Activity sheet – Triggers 
+ 
1	 Circle the synonyms of ‘trigger’ in the five sentences below.
• Militarism can start when countries form armies to fight.
• When people are extremely devoted to their country, this can activate a feeling of 
nationalism.
• Imperialism causes a power imbalance when countries take over other nations.
• Alliances begin when countries make agreements or friendships to support each other 
against enemies. 
• The climate in Europe before World War I was so tense, all it took was one action to 
prompt the outbreak of war.
2	 Use each synonym for ‘trigger’ in a sentence. The first one has been done for you.
Synonym
Sentence
activate
It only took one harsh word to activate the argument that had been brewing.
set off
cause
generate
start 
prompt

Language of triggers 
A trigger is an an action, process or series of events that starts  
something. Think of a line of dominoes falling. The trigger is the  
force that pushes the first domino, which then knocks the  
next over, and then the next, and so on.

Resource sheet – Triggers 
The assassination of  
Archduke Franz Ferdinand 
World War I was begun by a literal trigger – the trigger of a gun, when Archduke Franz 
Ferdinand was assassinated on 28 June 1914. His murder is called an assassination 
because it was for political reasons, and because he was a public figure. 
The victim
Archduke Franz Ferdinand was heir to the 
empire of Austria-Hungary, which had taken 
over Bosnia in 1908.   
The assassin
The assassin was from a group of Serbian 
terrorists who felt that Bosnia should be 
part of Serbia rather than Austria-Hungary.
The scene of the murder
The murder took place when the Archduke 
visited Bosnia and Herzegovina to inspect 
his army on 28 June 1914. 
The crime scene
There were two crime scenes and two attempts at the assassination. The first attempt  
was a grenade attack, which injured the Archduke’s attendants but left him unharmed.  
The Archduke was on his way to hospital to visit those injured in the first attack when he 
was ambushed. He and his pregnant wife were both shot and killed. 
The result
A month after the Archduke’s assassination, Austria-Hungary declared war against Serbia. 
This was the beginning of World War I.

Viewpoints of World War I (1)
When the Serbian attacker pulled the trigger and assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, 
this also served as the trigger for war. Soon after the assassination, Austria-Hungary 
declared war on Serbia. Serbia was allied with Russia, a member of the Triple Entente. 
However, Austria-Hungary was a member of the Triple Alliance. These alliances meant that 
what started as a small conflict quickly escalated into a world war.

Resource sheet – Australia joins the war 
Should Australia get involved?
Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914. The British Empire had many colonies. 
When Britain entered the war, its colonies and former colonies felt they needed to defend 
their ally. 
Australia was a former colony of Britain, and one its allies. Many Australians felt that it was 
their duty (job) to defend Britain when it needed support in World War I. 
However, not everyone agreed that Australia should join the fighting. Each side had 
reasons for their viewpoint (opinion). 
Should Australia go to war?
YES
We should go to war because ...
1	 Many of us came from Britain.  
We should help defend the ‘mother 
country’.
2	 We need to help defend our ally.
3	 We are still part of the British Empire, 
so we need to do our bit.
4	 Britain’s King is Australia’s King –  
we have a duty to fight for King and 
country. 
5	 The war will soon be over.
6	 We need to fight against the Germans 
who invaded Belgium.
NO
We should NOT go to war because ...
1	 Australia is not in Europe – the fight 
does not affect us.
2	 Australia is no longer a colony of  
Britain.
3	 It will cost lots of money.
4	 It will cost many lives. 
5	 It is wrong to kill other people.
6	 Australia should look to the future and 
not be bound by the past.

Who joins the war?
When war broke out in Europe, men rushed to 
enlist (join) in the war across Europe and its 
colonies. Only men could enlist as soldiers and 
go to war. Women could only participate by 
working as nurses or providing support away 
from the battlefield. 
Australia joined the fighting in August 1914, and 
men were keen to enlist. The Australian army 
chose its best men to fight in Europe, and by the 
end of 1914 more than 50 000 men had enlisted. 
The army had high standards – men had to meet 
strict age, height and fitness requirements in 
order to join. This meant that thousands of men 
were rejected by the Australian military (army). 
Australia had a population of four million people by the beginning of 1914. From the  
820 000 who were the right age to go to war, the army recruited 50 000 of Australia’s best 
men to join the fight.

Resource sheet – Recruiting an army
The conscription debate (1)
There were a lot of reasons why Australian men wanted to join the army in 1914.  
These included:
• Men got paid to be soldiers.
• Everyone thought the war would be over in six weeks, so they’d be home by Christmas.
• It was a chance to go on an adventure.
• It was an opportunity to travel for free.
• Being a soldier was a way that men could support their King and country.
• Peer pressure – all their mates were signing up.
Australia joined the war in August 1914. By the end of the year, 50 000 Australians had 
joined the war. That meant that more than 10 000 men signed up each month. However, 
by April 1915 the number of men enlisting each month had dropped to 6000. 
In April 1915 Australian troops were fighting at Gallipoli in Turkey (Ottoman Empire).  
Many Australians were killed at Gallipoli. The Australian army needed new soldiers to 
replace those they had lost and keep their numbers strong. In July 1915 they made it 
easier to join the army by reducing the height and age limits. The change is shown below.
Minimum height
Age limit
August 1914
168 cm (5 feet 6 inches)
19–38 
July 1915 
157 cm (5 feet 2 inches)
18–45
Some people believed that men should be forced to join the war. This would mean that all 
men of the right age could be forced to sign up. This is called conscription. 
Australians had to vote on the idea of introducing conscription. Debates were held, where 
people argued for and against conscription. There were two public votes – one in 1915 
and one in 1917. 
Australians were divided almost equally on the issue of conscription, and both votes were 
very close. However, the majority of Australians valued the freedom for men to choose 
whether or not to go to war, and both votes failed. Conscription was not introduced, and 
joining World War I remained a choice for Australian men.

Activity sheet – Propaganda
Defining propaganda 
Propaganda is information used to support a single point of view. This is called presenting 
a biased or unbalanced viewpoint. Here are two opposing, unbalanced viewpoints of 
Australia’s involvement in World War I: 
• Australia is not in Europe – 
the fight does not affect us.
• Australia is no longer a 
colony of Britain.
• It will cost lots of money.
Propaganda uses persuasive language to persuade the reader to agree 
with its point of view. Propaganda during World War I was designed to 
make people love their country and hate the enemy. 
+ 
1	 Sort the words in the word bank into ‘my country’ and ‘enemy 
country’ to show how you would use persuasive language to 
help the war effort.

• Many of us came from Britain, 
we need to defend the ‘mother 
country’.
• We should help defend our ally.
• As we are still part of the British 
Empire, we need to do our bit.

60
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The creation of the Anzacs
Biographies of Anzacs (1)
The Anzacs were the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. All the men were 
volunteers who chose to go to war. Some even lied about their age so they could join  
the fight.
The Anzacs’ first major battle was the landing at Gallipoli in Turkey (Ottoman Empire)  
on 25 April 1915. They had to jump off boats and run onto the beaches. They were running 
into a strange environment, wearing full military uniform. In these difficult conditions 
Australians quickly gained a toughness, or resilience. 
The Anzac troops quickly developed a reputation as soldiers who looked out for  
their mates, were brave and willing to sacrifice their lives to defend Australia and the 
British Empire. 
Anzacs who fought in World War I came from many different backgrounds, and joined 
the war for different reasons. The biographies of soldiers can help us to understand their 
different experiences. 
Biography of an Indigenous Australian 
Albert Knight (1894–1973) 
Albert Knight was born in March 1894 on Toorale station near Louth, New 
South Wales. He joined the Australian Imperial Force in November 1914, 
the second of three brothers to fight in World War I. 
Albert served in Belgium, where he was a bombing specialist and a noted 
scout. He stepped on a bomb in May 1918, but returned to the war after 
recovering from his injuries. In September 1918 he advanced 183 m 
across the battlefield in broad daylight, found the enemy’s weapons and 
destroyed them. This won him the Victoria Cross. 
He returned to Australia in July 1919 and went back to bush work in New 
South Wales, where he died in 1973. 

Achieve!   History – World War I – Book 1
61
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Resource sheet – The creation of the Anzacs
Biographies of Anzacs (2)
Biography of a young Australian-born soldier
Jim Martin (1901–1915) 
Jim Martin was born in the same year that Australia became an independent 
country. He went to war out of a sense of duty. 
He landed at Gallipoli in October and immediately became sick because of 
the poor hygiene and terrible conditions. He was taken to a hospital ship, 
but died and was buried at sea. He was 14. The official joining age was 18. 
Biography of an immigrant Australian 
John Simpson Kirkpatrick (1892–1915) 
John Simpson Kirkpatrick was born in Britain. He moved to Australia and 
joined the Australian Imperial Force in August 1914. He was killed in action 
on 19 May 1915, having taken part in the Gallipoli landing. 
Simpson was a stretcher-bearer during the Gallipoli campaign. His job  
was to transport wounded soldiers using a donkey and working under 
sniper-gun fire. He was killed while carrying two wounded men under 
machine-gun fire. 
Biography of an Australian army nurse
Clare Deacon (1891–1952) 
Clare Deacon was born on 13 March 1891 at Pipers River, Tasmania. She 
was the daughter of a farmer. 
Clare trained as a nurse at Hobart Hospital and passed her general nursing 
exam in 1912. She enlisted in the Australian Imperial Force in 1914, and 
was deployed as a staff nurse in the Army Nursing Service. She was posted 
to Egypt and served at Mena during the Gallipoli campaign. 
Clare worked in France from December 1915. She was awarded the Military 
Medal for bravery under fire after running into a bombed hospital building 
and getting the patients to safety, risking her life in the process. She 
returned to Australia in 1918, where she died of meningitis in 1952.

Activity sheet – The creation of the Anzacs
Where Australians fought in World War I
When Australians joined World War I they were fighting as part of the British Empire, 
which spanned a quarter of the world’s surface and controlled a third of the world’s 
resources. The British Empire was allied with the French and Russian empires, and was also 
fighting against the empires of Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman (Turkey). 
Most battles were fought away from Britain and Germany, in countries such as France and 
Turkey. This was to ensure that if they lost a battle, their home territory would not be taken 
over. Australians fighting in World War I were sent to different locations all around the world. 
The graves and memorials for the Anzacs who fought in these places are still there today.
+ Colour in the places where Australians fought in World War I on the map below. 
Look up the countries in an atlas if you cannot find them on the map.
Locations Australians fought and died in during World War I:

France
Palestine
United Kingdom
Belgium
Lebanon
Greece
Syria

Achieve!   history – World War i – Book 2
5
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Gallipoli
Background
The Anzac legend was born out of the tough 
conditions that Australian and New Zealand troops 
fought under at Gallipoli in Turkey. More than 20 000 
Anzacs landed on the beaches of Gallipoli at dawn 
on 25 April 1915. While Australians went on to fight 
campaigns on the Western Front and in the Middle 
East, it was at Gallipoli that the Anzacs established 
their military identity. 
Those recruited into the Australian Imperial Force were 
sent to Egypt to stop the threat of Turkey (formerly 
the Ottoman Empire) to the British in the Middle East. 
Australians were deployed to the Gallipoli Peninsula 
in April 1915 with the goal of taking over the Turkish 
capital, Constantinople. They were accompanied by 
troops from New Zealand, France and Britain. 
After the Australians landed at what is now referred 
to as Anzac Cove, there was fierce fighting between 
Australian and Turkish troops. Most attempts to gain 
territory ended in failure for both sides, and this 
stalemate continued throughout 1915. When the 
Australians retreated on 19–20 December they had 
achieved the most effective campaign of Gallipoli, as 
the Turkish troops did minimal damage to the Anzac 
troops compared to the losses they inflicted during 
earlier battles. 
Starter activity
Begin by showing the class images of Anzac Day 
celebrations in Australia and Turkey. Ask students to 
identify the locations of the Anzac Day services and to 
consider why the service takes place at dawn on this 
day each year. 
Before beginning the unit, hold a class discussion 
about the importance of perspective – how does 
being on a particular side effect how you see events? 
Allow students to explore the concept of bias in their 
own lives and how this can affect their judgement and 
choices. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Australian perspectives at Gallipoli 
(1)’, gives students the background to the Gallipoli 
campaign and presents an Australian’s perspective on 
the campaign.  
In the Activity sheet, ‘Australian perspectives at 
Gallipoli (2)’, students answer questions to help them 
analyse sources in order to gain an understanding of 
Australian perspectives. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Turkish perspectives at Gallipoli 
(1)’, offers students an alternative interpretation by 
identifying the Turkish perspective of the Gallipoli 
campaign. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Turkish perspectives at Gallipoli 
(2)’, encourages students to consider the Turkish 
perspective by answering questions about the sources. 
The final Activity sheet, ‘Bias and historical 
interpretation’, provides students with the ability to 
identify bias in historical interpretations. 
Extension ideas
• Students could view the 1981 Australian film 
Gallipoli, directed by Peter Weir, and create character 
profiles of the soldiers presented in the film in order 
to gain a deeper understanding of the perspectives 
of Anzacs who fought at Gallipoli.
• Note: It would be worth pointing out inaccuracies 
in the film, such as the little British command at 
the Nek, to students so that they are aware of the 
differences between cinema and historical record.
• Students could research the number of casualties/
deaths sustained by other nations at Gallipoli, such 
as India, New Zealand, Great Britain and Germany. 
Objectives
• To identify where Australians fought
• To understand the type of warfare used at 
Gallipoli
• To understand different perspectives
• To understand different historical 
interpretations
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

11
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Anzacs on the Western Front 
Background
In March 1916, after the Gallipoli campaign, the 
Anzacs were sent to France, having proven their 
abilities in battle. They served on the Western Front, 
where Germany had invaded Luxembourg, Belgium 
and France until their advance was stopped by Triple 
Entente forces. Both sides reached a line that remained 
largely unchanged for most of the war – indeed, from 
1916 to 1917, the warring sides advanced only metres 
at a time. It was only when America joined the war in 
1917, fighting with the Triple Entente, that there was any 
major change. The victorious Triple Entente pushed for 
Germany’s surrender on 11 November 1918. 
For Australia, this victory came at a particularly high 
cost. Australia’s casualty rate was almost 65% – the 
highest in the British Empire. Of the 60 000 Australians 
(nearly all men) who died fighting in World War I,  
45 000 were killed on the Western Front. 
Starter activity
Show students a map of the Western Front. Ask them 
how they would feel if they were fighting a war but 
were unable to move forward and gain territory. Would 
they feel like continuing, or would they feel frustrated 
and unfulfilled? 
Resource and Activity sheets
In the Activity sheet, ‘The Western Front’, students 
complete a cloze activity describing the location of  
the Western Front and explaining the purpose of the 
line there.  
The Resource sheet, ‘The Anzac spirit (1)’, discusses 
the role of the Anzacs on the Western Front and the 
qualities that the Australian soldiers showed in battle. 
The Activity sheet, ‘The Anzac spirit (2)’, introduces 
vocabulary used to describe the Anzacs. Students 
find synonyms and draw pictures to show their 
understanding. They then use these synonyms in a 
sentence describing the Anzacs. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Asking questions (1)’, shows 
students how the terms used in questions indicate the 
required response. Students learn to identify what a 
question is asking them to show in their responses.
In the Activity sheet, ‘Asking questions (2)’, students 
apply the vocabulary modelled on the Resource sheet, 
phrasing essay questions about the qualities of the 
Anzacs. They then answer the questions they have 
constructed. 
Extension ideas
• Students could choose one of the essay questions 
they responded to in the ‘Asking questions’ 
Resource and Activity sheets and expand their 
response into a longer essay or a class presentation. 
They could also undertake a second response to 
show how changing the language term used in the 
question will change their response. 
• Students could access film texts such as Blackadder 
Goes Fourth, to help them identify the mentality 
of the men in the trenches and the futility of the 
battles on the Western Front.
Objectives
• To identify where Australia fought
• To understand the Anzac legend
• To be able to use key terms and concepts
• To understand historical questions
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

Achieve!   history – World War i – Book 2
17
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Fighting on the frontline
Background
With World War I came the emergence of trench warfare 
as the standard method of fighting. Trench warfare 
signalled a stalemate in a conflict, but for the soldiers, 
life in the trenches was hell on Earth. Soldiers faced 
certain death if they went ‘over the top’ of the parapet, 
running directly into machine-gun fire from the enemy 
trenches. Even when staying in their own trench, they 
were constantly under attack from enemy shells or 
snipers. If they managed to survive this they had to 
contend with the rats, lice and mud that infested the 
trenches and caused diseases such as trench fever, 
trench nephritis and trench foot. The freezing winter 
on the Western Front took the lives of many men. This 
significant loss of manpower meant that it was left to 
nurses and the use of new technology to support the 
remaining soldiers on the frontline. 
Starter activity
Show students an image of the trenches. Ask them to 
describe the environment in which the soldiers fought 
and lived, using the following questions to guide the 
discussion:
• What is the environment like?
• What would it feel like to live there?
• How would this affect your motivation to fight? 
Examples of image sources:
• www.bbc.co.uk/history/worldwars/wwone/launch_
vt_trench_life.shtml
• www.abc.net.au/news/2012-04-20/anzacs-in-the-
front-line-trenches-during-wwi/3963124
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource Sheet, ‘Life in the trenches’, helps 
students understand the nature of trench warfare, the 
environment in the trenches and the implications this 
had for the health of the soldiers. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Describing life in the trenches’, 
encourages students to describe the environment in 
the trenches, using adjectives and poetry to convey 
the conditions. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘A soldier’s report’, students take 
on the perspective of a soldier living in the trenches 
during World War I, reporting on the experience of 
World War I in their own words. 
The Activity sheet, ‘The role of nurses’, explores the 
contribution of nurses through image analysis.  
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Technology in war’, students 
gain an understanding of how advances of technology 
helped the soldiers in battle. 
Extension ideas
• Students could explore the issue of the recognition 
of nurses during World War I and in subsequent 
conflicts. Possible questions to explore could be:
– Why hasn’t the contribution of nurses in World 
War I been recognised? 
– Was their contribution to World War I as 
important as that of the soldiers?
• Students could present their ideas in writing, giving 
reasons for their opinion, or they could participate 
in a class debate. Possible debate topics include:                
– Nurses should be recognised as soldiers
– Soldiers are the most important people in a war
– Women should not be involved in war 
• Students could conduct research to find modern 
versions of the technologies shown on the 
final Activity sheet. Students could track the 
development of these military technologies to 
explore how they changed to meet the needs of 
soldiers in battle over different wars. Examples to 
research include tanks, poison gas and machine 
guns. 
Objectives
• To be able to describe the types of warfare 
during World War I
• To be able to use different forms of 
communication
• To understand different perspectives
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

are still functional before use with students.

23
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Recording war experiences
Background
World War I was fought by everyday people who 
had to endure and survive terrible experiences. The 
primary sources they left behind, such as poems and 
letters home, help us to understand their experiences. 
By analysing these sources, we can learn more about 
the human experiences of World War I. 
Starter activity
Begin by asking students how they would feel fighting 
on the frontline as a soldier. Encourage them to 
consider the following questions:
• How would they feel living in the trenches? 
• How would they pass their free time? 
• Would they miss their family and friends? 
• How would they record their experiences?
Connect the idea of writing letters, journals and poetry 
to the modern equivalent of using social media to 
record experiences and reach out to friends and family. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘War poetry’, introduces poetry 
as a form of expression for soldiers on the frontline 
in World War I. Students identify the meaning or 
synonym of key words in a selected poem in order to 
better understand the poem’s main point. 
In the Resource and Activity sheets, ‘Journal entries (1) 
and (2)’, students read an extract from the journal of an 
Australian soldier, then answer questions analysing the 
information and exploring how the soldier was feeling 
at the time.
The Activity sheet, ‘Analysing sources’, has students 
identify the perspective of writers of two different 
sources, giving evidence for each author’s feelings.  
This allows students to document and compare the 
two perspectives. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Writing a letter home’, 
students apply the vocabulary and emotions they 
have been exposed to in the unit and create their own 
letter home, written from the perspective of a soldier 
fighting in World War I. Sentence starters are provided 
to help students organise and communicate their 
ideas. Students will need a sheet of paper to plan and 
write their final letters. 
Extension ideas
Students could write letters from different 
perspectives to compare the experiences of soldiers 
fighting in different conflicts, such as at Gallipoli and 
the Western Front. 
Objectives
• To use sources to understand the type of 
warfare during World War I
• To understand different perspectives
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

29
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Keep the home fires burning
Background
During the war a large proportion of the male 
population went to fight in World War I. The 
communities left behind had to function without 
these men and needed to keep up their morale 
despite constant reports of soldiers being killed. 
With men gone to the frontline, women were also 
given new work in order to support the war effort. 
In Australia, people who were from enemy countries 
were detained for the duration of the war to protect 
the home front. 
Starter activity
Begin by introducing the concept of morale 
with students – explain that it involves feelings 
of confidence, optimism and self-esteem, and 
encourage students to make connections to their own 
experiences. Brainstorm situations when morale is 
needed and what forms this can take. Role-play these 
situations with students to help them understand the 
importance of morale, and how it can affect behaviour 
and outcomes. 
Resource and Activity sheets
In the first Activity sheet, ‘Keeping up morale’, students 
explore the devices that were used to boost morale on 
the home front, such as songs and slogans. 
The Activity sheet, ‘News from the front’, helps students 
to understand and empathise with the impact on the 
community when they received news of a death on 
the frontline. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Enemies in Australia’, students 
describe the experiences of people from other 
countries who were interned in Australia during World 
War I. 
The Resource sheet, ‘Women and the war effort (1)’, 
describes the role of women in supporting the war 
effort, including fundraising and nursing. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Women and the war effort 
(2)’, students check their comprehension of the 
Resource sheet by answering literal, inferential and 
evaluative questions, which increase in difficulty. 
Extension ideas
• Students could create a poster promoting the 
importance of contributing to the war effort on 
the home front. This could employ strategies such 
as slogans or song lyrics to make the poster eye-
catching. The poster could appeal to or directly 
address women in order to convince them to 
contribute to the war effort. 
• Students could listen to recordings of songs  
from the era. Numerous original recordings can  
be found on the internet.  For example:  
www.firstworldwar.com/audio/index.htm
Objectives
• To understand the impact of war 
• To describe the changing role of women and 
the conscription debate 
• To use key terms and concepts
• To identify and respond to different kinds  
of questions
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check them 
for inappropriate content and to ensure that they 
are still functional before use with students.

35
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Turning the tides
Background
By 1917 World War I had been waged for nearly four 
years. Both sides of the conflict had suffered huge 
losses. Soldiers were tired of fighting a war that most 
people had assumed would be ‘over by Christmas’ 
back in 1914. Despite the success of the British naval 
blockade of Germany, the Triple Entente was starting 
to fall apart. The French suffered a mutiny and the 
Russians pulled out of the war after a revolution in 
Russia. It was the entry of America in April 1917 that 
sustained the Triple Entente and helped them force 
the Germans to surrender. The resulting armistice 
between leaders, which was signed in a railway 
carriage, came into force at 11 am on  
11 November 1918. 
Starter activity
Ask students how they would feel doing the same 
assignment for three years without a break, and 
without any evidence that they were doing well. 
Ask students to suggest emotions and list them on 
the whiteboard. Expand vocabulary by asking for 
associated words or synonyms, e.g. frustrated – tired – 
annoyed – upset. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘Three years at war’, helps 
students understand the experiences and frustration 
of soldiers as they entered the fourth year of World 
War I.
The Activity sheet, ‘The British naval blockade of 
Germany’, explores the naval blockade from both 
British and German perspectives. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘The Triple Entente stumbles’, 
students complete a cloze exercise describing what 
happened to the Triple Entente. 
The Activity sheet, ‘America joins in’, explains how 
America’s contribution helped the Triple Entente. 
Students complete a true/false activity to consolidate 
their understanding.
In the final Activity sheet, ‘The end, the armistice’, 
students explain the armistice from the perspective 
of an Australian soldier who is a veteran of the 1915 
Gallipoli campaign. 
Extension ideas
• Students could write a diary entry from the 
perspective of a German soldier who has spent 
three years on the Western Front, documenting their 
reaction to the armistice. Students could compare 
this to the Australian perspective explored on the 
Activity sheet, ‘The end, the armistice’, and analyse 
the similarities and differences. 
Objectives
• To understand the type of warfare in World  
War I
• To identify the perspectives of people from the 
past
• To use key terms and concepts
• To use different communication forms 
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

41
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Peace at last
Background
The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919.  
The terms of the treaty were particularly harsh in 
response to the French and British desire to see 
Germany punished for its part in starting World War 
I. The treaty had 440 clauses, which stipulated that 
Germany would accept sole responsibility for starting 
the war, have part of its territory taken away, pay other 
countries back for the damage it caused and have its 
army reduced. This punishment was designed to ensure 
that Germany could never start a war again. Other Triple 
Alliance countries such as Austria, Hungary and Turkey 
also had parts of their territory taken away. This land was 
turned into new countries or given to countries on the 
winning side that helped make the treaty. The Treaty of 
Versailles resulted in both winners and losers, depending 
on which side countries were on during the war. 
Starter activity 1
Encourage students to predict the terms of the treaty 
that would end World War I. 
• Will the winners punish the losers? 
• Will the treaty be a chance to punish the country 
that started the fight? 
• Will the treaty be fair to both sides? 
Starter activity 2 
Familiarise students with the terms of the Treaty of 
Versailles with a running dictation activity. This activity 
is focused on group work, team-building skills and 
speaking and listening skills in low literacy students. 
In your role as the teacher, concentrate on the:
• preparation (student analysis of text)
• dictation (do students speak slowly and clearly?)
• reconstruction (effective teamwork) 
1 Introduce students to the terms of the Treaty of 
Versailles (see Activity sheet, ‘Terms of the treaty’). 
Ensure that students understand the key concepts 
and vocabulary in the text.
2 Put students into groups and appoint a scribe for 
each group (this should be the most confident 
speller). 
3 Display the terms of the treaty at the front of the 
room, or place numerous copies around the room. 
4 Students must take it in turns to go up to the text 
and memorise as much of it as they can before 
returning to their group and dictating this to the 
scribe. When the scribe has finished writing, the next 
person can go. 
5 When the entire text has been dictated, the groups 
sit together to edit their text for spelling, grammar 
and punctuation.
6 The groups are assessed on their accuracy and 
speed in completing the task.  
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles (1)’, 
explains the purpose of the treaty that formally ended 
World War I for Germany. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles (2)’, 
students unjumble key words from the Resource sheet, 
then use each one in a sentence to demonstrate their 
understanding. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Examining the treaty’, helps 
students evaluate the treaty by asking literal, 
inferential and evaluative questions about its purpose. 
The Activity sheet, ‘Terms of the treaty’, helps  
students assess the terms of the treaty from two 
differing perspectives. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Mapping treatment under the 
treaty’, students identify the territory gained, lost and 
created under the terms of the treaty. 
Extension ideas
To further explore the different perspectives on 
the treaty, students could role-play an interview 
between representatives of different countries to help 
them understand different perspectives. Questions 
discussed could include:
• What was the purpose of the treaty?
• Do you think the treaty was fair?
• What do you think will be the long-term 
consequences of the treaty? 
Objectives
• To be able to describe the impact of World War I
• To understand different historical 
interpretations
• To understand different perspectives
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

47
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Consequences of the treaty
Background
World War I had consequences for all of society. The 
loss of men during the war had repercussions for 
families, communities and nations. The Germans 
saw the Treaty of Versailles as unfair, and the harsh 
punishment Germany had received sowed the seeds 
for revenge and the commencement of World War II. 
The weakening of Europe throughout the war also 
enabled America to dominate global politics as the 
new world power. 
Starter activity
Encourage students to consider how society could 
return to normal after World War I. Brainstorm issues 
that might arise in a society after a war has just ended, 
such as food shortages, unemployed men and injured 
or disabled returning soldiers. Have students suggest 
ways in which these challenges to society could be 
resolved. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity sheet, ‘The loss of men’, helps students 
to understand how the loss of men in the war affected 
families, communities and Australia as a whole. 
The Activity sheet, ‘A harsh punishment’, helps students 
understand Germany’s perspective on the punishment 
they received, and how this motivated them to seek 
revenge during World War II. 
The Resource sheet, ‘America becomes the new world 
power’, examines how World War I shifted the balance 
of power throughout the world, leaving European 
countries weakened and having to rebuild, while 
America enjoyed a time of great prosperity. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘How did America become the 
new world power?’, students form an argument 
outlining how America gained new power by 
presenting a main idea, providing evidence and 
examples, and linking these back to the topic of the 
treaty and World War I. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘The good times in America’, 
students examine two source images and extract 
information about America in the 1920s and its policy 
of self-preservation.  
Extension ideas
Students could track America’s rise to power, from 
its early beginnings to global dominance. Research 
questions could include:
• Who founded America?
• What made America richer after the war?
• What technologies did America create after World 
War I? 
• What was it like to live in America after the war? 
• Why did Europe take a long time to recover from 
World War I?
Objectives
• To be able to explain the type of warfare during 
World War I
• To understand different perspectives
• To use information from sources as evidence  
in argument
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

53
© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – From soldier to civilian
Background
Soldiers returning home from World War I had to 
adapt to the civilian life that they had left behind. 
Many were haunted by the mental and physical scars 
of war and found it hard to return to their old lives. 
While some support, such as the Soldier Settlement 
Scheme, was given to returning soldiers to help them 
find new roles, most soldiers found it difficult to adjust 
after witnessing the horrors of war. 
Starter activity
Conduct a ‘think, pair, share’ activity regarding the 
concept of returning home. Questions to prompt 
thinking could include: 
• What does ‘returning home’ mean? 
• Could a soldier ever forget seeing his friends die on 
the battlefield? 
• How might they feel about having killed someone?
• Do you think a soldier could return to their old life? 
Why/why not? 
Encourage students to make connections between 
World War I soldiers and those returning from current 
conflicts. 
Resource and Activity sheets
The first Activity Sheet, ‘Returning home’, helps 
students understand the transition of soldiers from 
World War I to their civilian lives. 
In the Activity sheet, ‘Senses in war’, students describe 
the experiences soldiers went through by exploring 
how each of the five senses were affected during the 
war and at home. 
The Resource sheet, ‘The roles of World War I veterans 
(1)’, presents images of returning soldiers in their new 
civilian roles, offering students an insight into the lives 
they were adapting to.
In the Activity sheet, ‘The roles of World War I veterans 
(2)’, students analyse the pictures from the Resource 
sheet in order to gain a better understanding of the 
returning soldiers’ experiences. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Interview with a World  
War I veteran’, students design an interview with 
a World War I veteran, listing questions to ask and 
enhancing these with a mix of literal, inferential and 
evaluative questions. 
Extension ideas
• Students could role-play their interview from the 
Activity sheet, ‘Interview with a World War I veteran’, 
with a partner.
• Students could interview a veteran from a more 
recent conflict and link their experiences of 
returning home to those of World War I veterans.
Objectives
• To describe the impact of World War I 
• To ask questions that help us to understand  
the past
• To evaluate sources
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities.

© Kate Crowhurst and Blake Education 2013
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – We will remember them
Background
Across the world people commemorate the end 
of World War I on 11 November each year. Known 
as Remembrance Day, this marks the date that 
World War I ended. People observe one minute of 
silence at 11 am on this date. Remembrance Day 
also commemorates those who suffered or died in 
subsequent wars. In the week before Remembrance 
Day people wear red poppies because these were 
the flowers that grew on the battlefields where the 
soldiers gave their lives. Wearing a poppy shows that 
we remember them. 
Australians observe Anzac Day on 25 April each year to 
remember the contribution of the Australian and New 
Zealand (Anzac) army. This was the day the Anzacs 
landed at Gallipoli and proved themselves in battle. 
On this day Australians remember the 8000 Australian 
soldiers who were killed at Gallipoli and celebrate the 
Anzac legend. 
Starter activity
Play students a sample of ‘The Last Post’, which is 
played on Anzac Day during dawn services. 
• Ask students how the music made them feel. Help 
them to recognise and articulate the emotions they 
experienced. 
• Ask students to identify whether they have heard 
the music before, and where. 
• If students have not heard the music before, ask 
them to predict why it was written and what it 
would be used for in connection to World War I.
• Explain the place of ‘The Last Post’ in Anzac Day 
dawn service ceremonies – after The Ode and 
before ‘Lest we forget’ is spoken. 
• ‘The Last Post’ can be downloaded at:  
www.awm.gov.au/commemoration/customs/last_
post.asp
Resource and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘How we remember (1)’, introduces 
scenes of remembrance for World War I soldiers, 
showing images of Remembrance Day and Anzac Day 
services. 
The Activity sheet, ‘How we remember (2)’, asks 
students to analyse the images on the Resource sheet. 
This information will also be used to strengthen the 
students’ arguments in their work on the Activity 
sheet, ‘Is remembering World War I important?’. 
In the Resource sheet, ‘The significance of the Anzac 
legend (1)’, students explore differing perspectives 
regarding whether or not Anzac Day is important to 
Australians. 
The Activity sheet, ‘The significance of the Anzac 
legend (2)’, encourages students to form their own 
opinion about the Anzac legend, prompting them to 
question both sides of the debate presented on the 
Resource sheet. 
In the final Activity sheet, ‘Is remembering World War 
I important?’, students consider the importance of 
remembering World War I and provide evidence for 
their opinion, referring to the Resource sheet, ‘How we 
remember (1)’. Students should refer to their analysis 
on the Activity sheet, ‘How we remember (2)’, to 
support their argument. 
Extension ideas
• Students could adapt their argument from 
the Activity sheet, ‘Is remembering World War I 
important?’, into an oral presentation.
• Students could use ICT to create a brochure, poster 
or blog to promote Anzac Day. Information could be 
sourced from the local RSL, museums and online.
Objectives
• To describe the commemoration of World  
War 1
• To understand the significance of the  
Anzac legend 
• To use information from a range of sources
• To use different forms of communication
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge to complete 
these activities. 
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Resource sheet – Gallipoli
Australian perspectives at Gallipoli (1)
Anzac stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. All the men in the Anzacs 
had volunteered to fight in World War I, and many were leaving Australia for the first time. 
At first it must have seemed like an adventure, a free trip around the world, but the troops 
were soon faced with the harsh realities of war. 
In April 1915 the Anzacs were deployed to the Gallipoli Peninsula with the goal of taking 
over the then Turkish capital, Constantinople. As soon as the Australians landed at Anzac 
Cove, fierce fighting broke out between Australian and Turkish troops. Most attempts to 
gain territory ended in failure for both sides. This stalemate continued throughout 1915. 
Source 1
This photo was taken at Gallipoli, Turkey, 22 
May 1915. It shows Australian soldiers from 
the 4th Battalion having their breakfast. 
Photographer unknown. Courtesy, Australian 
War Memorial H15685.
 
 
Source 2
This was written by Australian soldier Arthur Taylor. He is describing a night in Gallipoli in  
a letter to home. 
A pitch dark night and you standing in a narrow trench just wide enough to stop your 
shoulders from rubbing the sides, you can only see a handsbreadth in front of your face 
you hear the hiss of bullets passing overhead you cannot strike a match as the flare 
might cost one of your mates his life you move silently along pass the Officer on Duty he 
is muffled up to the eyes for the cold is bitter you look on one platform and there is the 
machine gun stripped of his outer casing ready to deal out death to any Turks that try to 
rush our trench we were only 40 yards apart. 
– Arthur Taylor
Source: Taylor, A H Manuscript held at the State Library of Victoria MS 12286

The text below is part of a tribute that Kemal wrote to the Anzacs who were killed at 
Gallipoli. He wrote it in 1934, the same year that he accepted the title ‘Atatürk’, which 
means ‘father of the Turks’. The changes Kemal initiated (made) during his 15 years as 
ruler made Turkey as modern as other countries, making him a hero to his people. 
In 1933, Kemal said, ‘I look to the world with an open heart full of pure feelings and 
friendship.’ The writing below can be found at the Kemal Atatürk Memorial on Anzac 
Parade in Canberra. 
Courtesy, Australian War Memorial P01141.001.
Those heroes that shed their blood and lost their lives... You are now lying in the soil of a 
friendly country. Therefore rest in peace. There is no difference between the Johnnies and 
the Mehmets to us where they lie side by side now here in this country of ours ... you, the 
mothers, who sent their sons from faraway countries wipe away your tears; your sons  
are now lying in our bosom and are in peace. After having lost their lives on this land.  
They have become our sons as well.
Note:
Johnnies – John and Johnny were common Australian names
Mehmets – Mehmet was a common Turkish name

Bias and historical interpretation 
History is the study of people and events from the past. When studying history, it is 
important to be aware of bias. This means being more likely to favour a particular point of 
view. Everyone has a favourite football team, TV show, type of music, etc. These preferences 
can affect, or bias, the way we judge other things. We need to recognise bias when looking 
at historical sources in order to form a balanced opinion.

Resource sheet – Anzacs on the Western Front 
The Anzac spirit (1)
The Anzacs had a difficult time on the Western Front. They were fighting in tough 
conditions, and neither side was winning or gaining any ground. 
The horrors of Gallipoli were repeated on an even larger scale at the Western Front. In their 
first battle with the Germans, 5533 Anzacs were killed or wounded. This was twice as many 
casualties as the Anzacs sustained at Gallipoli. 
Australia lost almost 65% of its men at the Western Front. This was the highest death 
rate of the British Empire. Of the 60 000 Anzacs killed in World War I, 45 000 were killed at 
the Western Front. A further 124 000 were wounded, and many carried the scars of the 
Western Front for the rest of their lives, suffering from health problems and disabilities. 
It was under these tough conditions, surrounded by allied forces, that the Anzacs 
demonstrated their true spirit to the rest of the world. Australian soldiers showed what 
it meant to be Australian. The diggers were known for their endurance, courage, good 
humour, larrikinism and mateship. In contrast to the British soldiers, the Anzacs became 
known for being irreverent (standing up to authority) and egalitarian (treating everyone 
equally, regardless of their rank or background). 
This photo shows 
Australian soldiers walking 
along a duckboard track 
in the Chateau Wood, 
part of the Western Front. 
Photograph taken 29 
October 1917. Courtesy, 
Australian War Memorial 
E01220.

Resource sheet – Fighting on the frontline
Life in the trenches
During World War I, trench warfare became the standard way for two sides to fight each 
other. A trench is a ditch or hole dug in the ground. Each side would hide in a trench to 
protect themselves from enemy gunfire and military shells. These trenches stretched all 
the way across the battlefield. The trenches of the Western Front spanned 764 km – this is 
almost the distance between Melbourne and Sydney (875 km). 
The idea of trench warfare was for most of the group to make it across to the enemy’s 
trench and take it over, gaining enemy territory. However, the invention of the machine 
gun meant that bullets could be fired very quickly. Soldiers faced certain death when they 
went ‘over the top’ of the trench. 
The area between the trenches was known as ‘no man’s land’. This was the piece of land 
the soldiers had to cross in order to get to the enemy’s trench. Many men died in ‘no man’s 
land’, and stretcher bearers could not always reach these men to carry their bodies away. 
If a soldier managed to avoid going ‘over the top’ they still had to survive living in the 
trenches. The underground bunkers the men lived in were freezing cold, and the rain at 
the Western Front caused a layer of mud, which soldiers had to stand in. 
Disease was widespread. The damp, cold mud caused trench foot – an infection of the feet 
which caused them to swell. Many soldiers had their feet amputated (removed) because 
of this disease. The crowded, damp conditions also meant that lice and rats spread across 
the trenches, causing diseases such as trench fever, which was carried by lice.

Technology in war
In order to minimise casualties (dead and wounded), both sides used technology to support 
their soldiers. Technology means making, changing and using equipment in order to achieve 
goals. War technology uses this equipment to help soldiers win the war as quickly and 
effectively as possible. Tanks and machine guns are examples of how technology can be 
used in war to harm the enemy without risking soldiers on the frontline.

Activity sheet – Recording war experiences
War poetry 
Soldiers who fought in World War I were forced to witness and carry out the killing of war. 
Many soldiers wrote poetry during the war to express and record their emotions.
+ 
1  Read the following poem written by Wilfred Owen, a soldier in World War I.
Dulce et Decorum Est 
by Wilfred Owen, October 1917 
Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, 
Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge, 
Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots 
But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind;
If in some dreams you too could walk 
Behind the wagon that we flung him in
My friend, you would not tell with such high zest 
To children ardent for some desperate glory, 
The old lie: Dulce et decorum est 
Pro patria mori.
(Please note, this is an edited version of the original poem.)

Resource sheet – Recording war experiences
Journal entries (1) 
People write journal (diary) entries during wars to record their experiences. The journal 
entry below was written by an Australian soldier at Gallipoli. 
Wednesday, 4 August 1915
The explosion of a bomb dropped by an enemy aeroplane woke me this 
morning just after dawn, it fell about 50 yards away an exploded with 
a deafening crash but did not damage. We have been engaged today 
constructing a sand bag shelter for a dressing station which is situated in our 
camp ... A large number of Kitcheners new army [a British army of volunteers, 
formed by Kitchener, the British Minister for War. They were fighting on the 
same side as Australia.] arrived here during the night ... Sixteen reinforcements 
[new soldiers sent to strengthen the army already fighting] arrived early this 
morning for our unit and one was wounded this afternoon while bringing 
water from the water depot. An enemy aeroplane passed over here at about 
6pm and followed one of our own machines down towards the Cape, and a 
little later another of our planes circled overhead for a while.
Source: Australian War Memorial: PR00039 – Papers of Herbert Vincent Reynolds. <http://www.awm.gov.au/blog/ 
2010/08/04/wednesday-4th-august-1915-diary-of-hv-reynolds/> 29 March 2013
Context:
•	 This journal entry was written by an Australian soldier, Private Herbert Vincent Reynolds, 
from Victoria. 
•	 Reynolds enlisted on his 18th birthday, as soon as he could legally join the army,  
on 16 September 1914. 
•	 The entry was written on 4 August 1915 in Gallipoli, where Reynolds had landed on  
25 April. 
•	 Reynolds was a stretcher bearer. He became ill and was evacuated on 16 August 1915.
•	 He served again during World War I in France and Belgium and was discharged from 
the army in 1919.

Activity sheet – Keep the home fires burning
Keeping up morale  
Many men left their homes to go and fight in World War I. As women, children and those 
who could not fight waited at home, it was vital that they remained positive about the 
war. We call this ‘keeping up morale’. 
One way people kept their morale up was by singing songs that were positive about the 
war. Examples of these are shown below:
‘Keep the Home Fires Burning 
(Till the Boys Come Home)’
Keep the home fires burning  
While your hearts are yearning, 
Though your lads are far away 
They dream of home, 
There’s a silver lining 
Through the dark clouds shining, 
Turn the dark clouds inside out, 
Till the boys come home.
‘Pack Up Your Troubles’
Smile, boys, that’s the style. 
What’s the use of worrying, 
It never was worthwhile, so 
Pack up your troubles in your old kit bag, 
And smile, smile, smile.
Note: a kit bag was a bag used to hold 
the kit, or war equipment, that soldiers 
carried with them.

When the people at home received news from the front, it was often informing them that

Mothers, sisters, wives and friends 
would receive an official letter 
notifying (telling) them that their 
loved one had died. The letter  
would start:     
It is my painful duty to  
inform you ...
It is my painful duty to inform you ...
Not many letters start this way. When an army branded letter or telegram arrived, people 
knew that someone in their community had been wounded, killed or was missing, and 
might never return to them.

Enemies in Australia 
When Australia joined the war on 4 August 1914, they were wary of the people living 
in Australia who came from enemy countries. Just one week after war was declared, all 
German citizens living in Australia were named ‘enemy aliens’. People from Turkey, Austria 
and Bulgaria were later given the same label. Enemy aliens were jailed until the war was 
over. People whose father or grandfather was from an enemy country were also jailed. 
Internment camps were set up for the enemy aliens around Australia until 1915, when 
all the prisoners were moved to Holsworthy, New South Wales. The internment camp at 
Holsworthy held 4000–
5000 prisoners. While the 
inmates were not free to 
leave, there were theatre 
and arts groups, cafes 
and education classes to 
prevent boredom.

Resource sheet – Keep the home fires burning
Women and the war effort (1) 
Before World War I broke out, a woman’s role was considered to be in the home. Women 
were raised to be wives and mothers rather than to have a career or get an education. 
However, with their husbands, fathers and brothers gone to war, women had to manage 
the household finances, resources and family responsibilities alone. Many also had to deal 
with the grief of losing loved ones. Some women started working in the food, clothing and 
print industries. 
Australian women actively contributed to the war effort in many ways. Some women 
raised money for charities such as the Red Cross, which sent home comforts like warm 
clothes to soldiers. Other women knitted socks and scarves for the soldiers. 
Many women became nurses with the Australian army. The Australian Army Nursing 
Service (AANS) sent more than 2300 female nurses to places all around the world, 
including Egypt, France and Turkey. Seven Australian women earned the Military Medal (a 
bravery medal for people who weren’t soldiers). 
Some women wanted to help in other roles, such as drivers or cooks in the army, but the 
Australian army would not allow this. 
Sister Rachael Pratt
1874–1954 (died aged 80) 
•	 Sister Pratt was a nurse. 
•	 She was born in Victoria. 
•	 She enlisted in the war on 5 May 1915.
•	 She looked after wounded soldiers at Gallipoli 
and worked in Egypt and France as an army nurse. 
•	 She was awarded the Military Medal for bravery 
under fire. In July 1917 a German bomb exploded, 
injuring Pratt. The shrapnel from the bomb cut 
into her back and punctured a lung. Despite her 
injuries, she kept caring for the soldiers until she 
collapsed. 
•	 Sister Pratt returned to Australia at the end of the 
war but had chronic bronchitis  (a lung infection).
c.1918. Courtesy, Australian War Memorial 
P05664.001.
ISBN 978 1 92209 065 2

questions.

Three years at war
By the start of 1917 the war had been going on for more than two years. When war broke 
out in July 1914 most people thought that it would be over by Christmas. But three 
Christmases later the war was still being fought, with no clear signs of victory for either side. 
Soldiers were fighting on the frontline in trenches filled with damp, cold mud, living with 
disease, rats and lice. Explosions from shells (bombs) were constant. Soldiers who survived 
the shells had to face ‘going over the top’ and running into the path of enemy machine-
gun fire as they tried to attack the enemy trenches.

The British naval blockade of Germany
The British navy was the most powerful navy in the world. They used their ships to block 
German ports immediately after war broke out in August 1914. This stopped Germany 
getting new goods from other countries.
British naval ships would patrol the North Sea and stop merchant ships who were 
delivering goods to Germany. The Germans launched a counter offensive, using 
submarines to sink British ships, but the British were assisted by their allies, who protected 
British ships by travelling in large convoys so they could defend themselves. 
The blockade worked. By 1915, German imports had fallen by 55% since the war began. 
This meant that Germans had to ration their food supplies, making everyday life very 
hard. This pressure reduced nationalism in Germany, making the German people less 
willing to keep fighting the war.

America joins in 
America is far from Europe, and had no ties to the countries that were fighting. At the start 
of World War I, the USA declared that it was neutral, and did not send its soldiers into 
battle. 
Americans disliked the Germans because of their submarine warfare. In February 1915 
German submarines started attacking merchant ships and non-army ships. In May 1915 
they sunk British-owned ship the Lusitania, an attack that killed thousands of passengers, 
including 128 Americans. 
The Germans continued to sink ships belonging to neutral countries because they were 
trading with Britain. As a result, America declared war on Germany in April 1917. American 
troops arrived in France in June 1917. These fresh soldiers represented a significant positive 
change, and a turning of the tides for the Triple Entente. By the time the war ended, more 
than 2 million American soldiers had served on the Western Front, helping the Triple Entente 
win the war.

The end, the armistice
Thanks to the Americans joining the fight in 1917, the Triple Entente grew stronger 
against the Triple Alliance. Germany was weakened by Britain’s continuing naval blockade. 
The German people were starving. They began holding strikes (stopping work) and  
anti-war marches to protest against the war. In September 1918 the German military 
leaders told the Kaiser (the German King) that the war was lost. The German navy 
mutinied in October and the Kaiser abdicated, or stepped down, on 9 November 1918. 
An armistice (peace agreement) was signed between the leaders of all the fighting 
countries on 11 November. It was signed in a railway carriage in France and came into 
effect at 11 am on 11 November 1918.

Achieve!
The Treaty of Versailles (1)
World War I officially ended at 11 am on 11 November 1918. However, the damage caused 
by a war that had dragged on for four years needed to be formally addressed by a treaty 
between the two sides. 
What was the Treaty of Versailles?
A treaty is an agreement between two sides to stop fighting. There was a different treaty 
for each member of the Triple Alliance. The Treaty of Versailles dealt with Germany. The 
treaty was signed at the Palace of Versailles in France on 28 June 1919. It created formal 
peace between Germany and the members of the Triple Entente.
Who was involved?
Germany was the target of the treaty, but it was not part of the talks about what should go 
into it. Only the Triple Entente and their allies were present. Some of the allies, especially 
France, wanted to see Germany punished harshly for its part in the war. 
Germany was presented with a finished treaty and forced to sign it because it had lost the 
war. Many people were angry with Germany, and the terms of the treaty were designed to 
punish Germany and make it weak so that it could not start another war. 
What was the outcome?
The outcome was the harsh punishment of Germany. The terms of the treaty stated that 
Germany must accept war guilt by saying it was to blame for starting the war. There were 
financial (money), military (army) and territory (land) losses for Germany. It also had to 
pay reparations – money paid to other countries to make up for the damage caused. The 
treaty also created an organisation in Europe called the League of Nations, which would 
make decisions and help control nations like Germany.

Terms of the treaty
The Treaty of Versailles included clauses (terms) that Germany had to agree to in order to 
make peace with other countries. This included five clauses:
1  A League of Nations was created. This was a group of nations who would work together

3  Germany had to pay money to other countries to make up for the damage caused

4  Military removal meant that Germany’s army and navy were restricted, and it was not 
allowed to have an air force. 
5  Land removal meant that much of Germany’s territory was given away to other countries.

A harsh punishment
Imagine your friend gets into a fight at lunchtime. You rush to help support them. More 
people join in, and eventually you lose the fight. The winner is allowed to pick your 
punishment, and they make you:
•	 accept the blame for starting the fight in the first place
•	 pay money for damages to others
•	 give up some of your possessions. 
+ 
1 How does this make you feel?  
 
 
2 Is this a fair punishment? Why/why not?  
 
 
 
 
3 Would you try to get revenge? Why/why not?  
 
 
 
 
This was how Germany felt after World War I. They had lost the war and could not fight 
back against the victorious Triple Entente, so they had to sign the treaty. 
Germany was humiliated (embarrassed). It was forced to accept all the blame for a war 
that had been building up for a long time. The money Germany had to pay for damage 
caused by the war took money away from the German war recovery. 
Many Germans were angry about this treatment. They wanted revenge on other countries 
and were eager to prove that Germany could be strong again. These feelings led to the 
outbreak of a longer and more widespread war in 1939 – World War II. 
4 Could Germany have just refused to sign the treaty? Why/why not?  
 
 
5 Why did World War II occur?

Resource sheet – Consequences of the treaty
America becomes the new world power
Most countries in Europe were left weakened by World War I. For years their lives had been 
focused on a war that was suddenly over. Communities had to rebuild after significant 
losses of men and resources. 
Empires such as the British Empire had been called world powers because they controlled 
much of the world. However, the losses they had sustained meant that many countries 
were no longer as powerful. Some empires, such as the German and Ottoman empires, 
were broken up entirely. This loss of territory meant they were no longer empires, and 
were simply called Germany and Turkey. 
One country, however, became more powerful after the war. This was America, who didn’t 
join the war until 1917.  
Despite joining the war late, the Americans lost thousands of men in the conflict.  
US President Wilson, who had made the decision to join the war, was defeated in the  
1920 election by Warren Harding. Harding believed that America should protect itself and 
not worry about outside events. He wanted America to stay out of the League of Nations, 
to limit immigration (people from other countries coming to live in America) and to give 
businesses more freedom. The American government had been controlling businesses 
during World War I in many ways, such as telling them what to produce (make).
President Harding’s election showed that most 
Americans wanted to make America stronger, 
rather than helping others in Europe. At the start 
of the 1920s, wages in America were higher than 
in Europe because their resources had not been 
dedicated to four years of war. People used this 
extra money to improve their lives by buying cars 
and new consumer appliances.

important
Statement: I believe that 
remembering the Anzacs is 
important.
•	 We should not forget the 
sacrifices that were made for 
Australia in World War I and  
that continue to be made by 
soldiers today.

celebrates what is great about 
Australians and what we think is

not important

remembering the Anzacs is

is no longer relevant, and is just 
an excuse for a public holiday.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
5
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Background
At the start of World War I (WWI) in 1914, Britain, 
France and Russia were allies. These nations formed 
the Triple Entente (Allied powers). Australia fought 
with them. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed 
the Triple Alliance (Axis powers). Italy changed sides 
during the war. The USA entered WWI in 1917 and 
fought with Britain, France and Russia. WWI was won 
by the Allied powers and Germany was defeated.
	
The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919. 
The newly formed Weimar Republic (government 
established in Germany after WWI) became 
increasingly unpopular with Germans because it had 
signed the treaty which demanded they pay Allied 
nations, especially France and Belgium, millions of 
dollars in war reparations. This discontent was seized 
upon by the newly formed Nazi Party. 
	
The Great Depression created international 
financial and social insecurity. Resultant 
unemployment helped Hitler and Mussolini rise to 
power. Japan, Germany and Italy increased territorial 
acquisitions to secure raw materials. Other nations 
could not afford to successfully implement sanctions 
to prevent this empire building.
Starter activity
Write these country names on the board: Austria-
Hungary, Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Italy. Work 
with the students to identify which nations belonged 
to the Triple Entente (Allied powers) and which 
belonged to the Triple Alliance (Axis powers). Remind 
students that each group was trying to prevent the 
other from building up military powers and annexing 
land, and that other nations fought with these groups.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles’, provides 
background information on the Treaty of Versailles, the 
treaty’s demands on Germany and Germany’s reaction. 
Read the sheet with the students and make sure they 
understand the meaning of each term shown in bold.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Understanding the 
Treaty of Versailles’, students will need the Resource 
sheet, ‘The Treaty of Versailles’, and a dictionary. 
Students will write definitions and complete a 
cloze activity to check their comprehension of the 
information on the Resource sheet.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Newspaper 
headlines’, students need to refer to a newspaper or 
online news site. Students choose the three most 
interesting headlines from the newspaper. Then they 
write three headlines of their own about the Treaty 
of Versailles from the perspectives of journalists from 
different nations. You could extend the activity by 
asking students to write the first few paragraphs in the 
news articles for the German and French journalists, or 
a journalist from another nation of their own choosing.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘The Great Depression 
and insecurity’, outlines how high unemployment, 
territorial expansion and a policy of appeasement 
contributed to WWII. Read the sheet with the students, 
and discuss the meaning of each term in bold. You 
could locate the countries mentioned on a world map. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Understanding the Great 
Depression’, asks students to recall basic information 
from the Resource sheet, ‘The Great Depression and 
insecurity’, and to fill in a timeline.
Extension idea
• Divide students into small groups and ask them 
to imagine they are at the Versailles Peace 
Conference. Have them present arguments about 
whether or not Germany should have to pay war 
reparations, and if so, how much they should pay.
Teacher’s notes – Contributing causes
Objectives
• To recognise German discontent with the 
Treaty of Versailles
• To develop an awareness of how the Great 
Depression contributed to WWII
• To understand the meanings of key words.
Prior knowledge
Students need to have an understanding of World 
War I, and the nations that fought on the different 
sides.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
11
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
 
Background
The term totalitarianism, was first used in the 1920s 
in reference to Italian Fascists. It is a political system 
that attempts to completely control both public and 
private life. Totalitarian governments control the media 
and use propaganda to promote their ideologies. 
They also rigorously control any opposition. Often 
totalitarian states are led by charismatic leaders who 
are dictators. Totalitarianism is not always synonymous 
with dictatorships; however, Hitler and Mussolini were 
dictators who formed totalitarian states. 
In the 1930s, Mussolini and Hitler worked towards 
developing totalitarian states. Mussolini aimed to 
restore Italy to her ancient glory. Under his leadership, 
Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935 and Albania in 1939. 
Hitler’s aim was to stop Germany paying further 
war reparations. He also wanted to increase German 
territory to create more living space for German 
nationals and to create the perfect Aryan race.
Starter activity
Write the word totalitarianism on the board. Explain to 
the students that totalitarianism is a political system 
that believes the government should have total 
control over people’s public and personal lives. 
Divide the board into two columns. In the first column, 
list other major systems of government. In the second 
column write a definition of each system (examples 
shown below).
System
Definition 
Democracy
The people or the people’s elected 
representatives govern.
Socialism
The means of production is mostly owned 
by the state to benefit the majority.
Communism
A system that is opposed to individuals 
owning capital. 
Encourage the students to share their opinions about 
each system of government.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘Totalitarianism’, provides a cloze 
activity explaining what totalitarianism is, and which 
nations had totalitarian governments in 1939. 
	
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Adolf Hitler’, with the 
students and ensure they understand the meanings 
of the terms in bold. This sheet outlines Hitler’s rise 
to power and his relationship with the Nazi Party, 
and introduces Hitler’s doctrine of the perfect race. A 
primary source in the form of a photo of Hitler is also 
provided.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Adolf Hitler and 
a primary source’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Adolf Hitler’. Students will answer 
comprehension questions about the information on 
the resource sheet, and respond to the photo of Hitler. 
	
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Benito Mussolini’, 
with the students and ensure they understand the 
meanings of the terms in bold. This sheet provides 
background information on Mussolini, his rise to 
power and his dictatorship. A primary source in 
the form of a photo of Mussolini and Hitler is also 
provided. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Hitler and 
Mussolini’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheets, ‘Adolf Hitler’ and ‘Benito Mussolini’. Students 
will complete a Venn diagram comparing Hitler and 
Mussolini, and write three observations about the 
photo of Mussolini and Hitler.  To extend the activity, 
you could ask students to write sentences about the 
similarities between Hitler and Mussolini.
Extension ideas
Students could go to this website: www.fresno.k12.
ca.us/divdept/sscience/history/totalitarianism.htm 
to learn more about the rise of totalitarianism. Guide 
the students’ reading by providing questions for them 
to answer, such as:
What type of dictatorship was set up in Japan by 1932? 
(Answer: a military dictatorship)
Why did Japan want an overseas empire?  
(Answer: to gain raw materials)
What north-eastern Chinese province did Japan 
invade? (Answer: Manchuria)
Teacher’s notes – Totalitarianism and dictators
Objectives
• To develop a basic understanding of 
totalitarianism
• To identify Hitler and Mussolini as dictators
• To gain an awareness of Japanese ambitions
• To examine primary source photos
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.
