17
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The rise of the Nazi Party
Background
The Nazi Party grew from a minor extreme right wing 
party in 1919 to one with millions of supporters in 
1939. Once under Hitler’s leadership, it ruthlessly 
quashed opposition and indoctrinated thousands. Its 
growth was greatly aided by German dissatisfaction 
with the terms of the Versailles Treaty and the high 
unemployment levels Germany experienced during 
the Great Depression.
Starter activity
Explore the idea of indoctrination by asking questions 
such as:
•  Have people ever made you believe that something 
is the best thing in the world?
•  How did these people make you believe this? For 
example, did they show you glossy photos, play great 
music or have a special group they wanted you to 
join? 
•  Did these people allow you to ask any questions?
Now provide students with the following definition of 
indoctrination:
Indoctrinate means to fill a person’s mind with beliefs 
and to not let a person question those beliefs.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘The National Socialist German 
Workers’ Party’, provides background information 
on the Nazi Party’s rise to power. It also introduces 
students to the machinery the party had in place to 
quash any opposition.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘The Nazi Party’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, ‘The 
Nationalist Socialist German Workers’ Party’. Students 
will identify statements as true or false, and complete a 
cloze activity. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Nazi Youth’, provides 
information about Hitler Youth. Students will match 
terms to definitions, and some students might want 
to use a dictionary. Then students will complete 
comprehension questions about the information on 
the page.  
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Nuremberg Rally – a secondary 
document’, asks students to respond to an illustration 
of German youth at the 1934 Nuremberg Rally. Make 
sure students understand the difference between a 
primary source and a secondary source. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Two different perspectives’, 
provides contrasting perspectives about living in 
Germany – one from a German teenager in 1934, 
and another from a Jewish German teenager in 1939. 
Students will answer questions about the teenagers’ 
stories.
Extension idea
Ask students to imagine they are Jewish teenagers 
in Germany in the 1935. Their best friend is German, 
and has just joined the Hitler Youth group or the 
League of German Girls. Have students write a letter 
to their friend, asking why they joined this group and 
explaining how they feel about it. Students could also 
work in pairs to reply to one another’s letters. 
Objectives
• To become familiar with background 
information about the Nazi Party
• To understand how the Nazi Party gained 
power
• To learn about the Hitler Youth
Prior knowledge
An awareness of how the Treaty of Versailles 
affected Germany (see Unit 1) would help 
students’ understanding of this unit.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
23
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Outbreak of war  
and Australia’s response
Background
On the 1st September, 1939, Germany invaded Poland. 
This contravened the terms of the Munich Agreement. 
Consequentially, on the 3rd September, 1939, Britain 
and France declared war on Germany. On the same 
date, the Australian Prime Minister, Robert Menzies, 
announced that because Britain was at war, Australia 
would also be at war.
Starter activity
Introduce the concept of Britain as Australia’s mother 
country prior to WWII. Explain to students that when 
WWI started, it was automatically assumed that if 
Britain was at war, Australia was also at war. At the start 
of WWII, the Australian government also supported 
‘the mother country.’ However, after the bombing of 
Pearl Harbour, there was a shift in attitudes towards 
supporting Britain.
Facilitate a discussion around the question:
Why did Australians look to Britain as ‘the mother 
country’ before and at the start of WWII?
Answer: Most non-Indigenous Australians were 
descendants of Britain. The majority of Australians 
viewed Australia as part of the British Empire. 
Australia’s political and legal systems were very similar 
to Britain’s. Australia also had strong economic ties 
with Britain.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘1939 Invasion of Poland’, outlines 
Hitler’s invasion of Poland, and Britain and France’s 
subsequent declaration of war. It also presents 
Menzies’ response to Britain’s involvement. You could 
have the students locate each country mentioned on a 
world map. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘The start of World 
War II’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘1939 Invasion of Poland’. Students will complete 
a definition exercise and comprehension questions.
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Australia’s response’, students 
will explore further the information about Australia’s 
reaction on the Resource sheet, ‘1939 Invasion of 
Poland’. Students will identify given statements as true 
or false and complete a cloze comprehension activity. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Opinions about Australia going 
to war’, asks students to respond to two different views 
about Australia entering WWII. 
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Forming alliances’, students 
will complete exercises about the major Axis powers 
and Allies in the early years of WWII.  
Answers: a countries, b bombing, c declare, d entered,  
e Sweden, f joined
Extension ideas
• 
Students could find Prime Minister Menzies’s 
speech from 3rd September, 1939. This speech 
begins: ‘It is my melancholy duty ...’ 
	
Students will find these websites useful:  
	
www.menziesvirtualmuseum.org.au/ 
1930s/1939.html 
www.awm.gov.au/encyclopedia/ 
prime_ministers/menzies.asp 
Ask students to write down the first sentence of 
the speech, and explain what they think it means. 
• 
Ask students to imagine that it is 3rd September, 
1939 and they have just heard Menzies’ speech. 
Remind students that in 1939, Australia and 
Britain were closely linked and that Australia had 
a strong import and export trade with Britain. 
Have students draw a self portrait with a caption 
explaining why or why not Australia should follow 
Britain to war.
 
Objectives
• To identify the immediate cause of WWII
• To explore Britain and France’s declaration of 
War on Germany
• To present Menzies’ response to the declaration 
of war
• To develop research skills
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

29
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Holocaust
Background
Hitler’s belief that Jews were ‘subhuman’ was revealed 
in his book Mein Kampf. Initially, people thought Hitler 
was crazy but as he rose to power, he gained millions 
of supporters. Under Hitler’s leadership, the Nazi Party 
constantly spread propaganda which undermined, 
persecuted and separated Jews and other non-Aryans. 
The Holocaust was the genocide of millions of Jews 
and other people Hitler considered ‘undesirable’.
 ‘The Final Solution’ refers to the Nazi policy that all 
European Jews be killed. This policy was developed 
in the early 1940s and was initially implemented by 
shooting Jews in the Soviet Union. From 1942, it was 
done in extermination camps.
Starter activity
Write the word ‘Holocaust’ on the board. Ask students 
what they think of when they hear this word, and list 
their ideas. Provide students with the definition: 
The Holocaust refers to the genocide of millions of 
Jews and Gypsies, and the murder of disabled people, 
Jehovah’s Witnesses, communists, homosexuals and 
other opponents of Hitler. 
Explain that genocide is the deliberate and planned 
extermination of a race of people.
Resource sheets and Activity Sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Hitler’s propaganda against Jews’, 
defines propaganda and anti-Semitism. It also outlines 
how racism against Jews was spread through the 
media, and Hitler’s persecution of Jews. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Propaganda’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘Hitler’s propaganda against Jews’. Students may need 
a dictionary to complete the definitions exercise. They 
will also complete a cloze activity. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘The Final Solution’, outlines 
the two stages of this Nazi policy. It also points out the 
other groups of people victimised by the Nazis, and 
explains what data is.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Examining the 
Holocaust’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘The Final Solution’. Students will complete 
comprehension questions and a cloze activity. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Euphemisms’, explains and 
provides examples of euphemisms. It also asks 
students to consider why Nazis used the euphemism 
‘The Final Solution’.
Extension ideas
• 
Have students select three of the words from 
the definitions exercise on the Activity sheet, 
‘Propaganda’,  and use each word in a separate 
sentence.
• 
The White Rose was a German resistance youth 
group opposed to Nazis. Students could refer to 
the following websites to find out more about this 
group. 
	
http://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/ 
Holocaust/rose.html
	
http://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/ 
nazis-arrest-white-rose-resistance-leaders
Objectives
• To understand the meaning of propaganda
• To learn how propaganda was used by the  
Nazi Party.
• To learn about the Nazi Party’s ‘Final Solution’.
Prior knowledge
An awareness of the rise of Hitler and the  
Nazi Party would be useful.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Concentration camps
Background
Much of the information on concentration camps and 
what happened to the people who were sent to such 
camps is too horrific to present to students. Therefore 
some details and images have been deliberately 
excluded from this unit. Between 1939 and 1945, Nazi 
concentration camps were established to imprison 
people the Third Reich considered to be ‘undesirables’. 
These camps were used as slave labour units. Millions 
died from starvation and diseases. Many were 
murdered.
Starter activity
As a class, write sentences about how the students 
would feel if they were sent away from their families 
to a concentration camp. Tell students that when they 
were first sent to such a camp, they probably would 
not have known what was going to happen to them. 
List these words on the board to help with composing 
the sentences: confused, angry, scared, worried, lonely.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
	
The Resource sheet, ‘What were Nazi concentration 
camps?’ defines concentration camps and provides 
information about Auschwitz, the largest Nazi 
concentration camp. Read the sheet with the students 
and make sure they understand the meaning of each 
term shown in bold. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘About 
concentration camps’, students will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘What were Nazi concentration 
camps?’. Students will answer comprehension 
questions and multiple choice questions to complete 
sentences.
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Writing sentences’, students 
will identify subjects and verbs in given sentences, 
then write their own sentences about concentration 
camps.  
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Children in concentration 
camps’ asks students to complete a cloze activity 
which provides information on children in 
concentration camps, and introduces David Kaplan 
and Anne Frank. 
	
The Activity Sheet ‘A primary source – Ebensee 
photo’, provides a primary source photo of boys freed 
from a concentration camp in 1945. Students will 
complete questions to guide their response to this 
photo.  
Extension ideas
• 
Students could work in pairs or individually to 
write five questions they would like to ask the 
boys in the photo on the Activity sheet, ‘A primary 
source – Ebensee photo’.
• 
Students could write a letter to Anne Frank or 
David Kaplan.
Objectives
• To learn about concentration camps
• To respond to a primary document
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The home front
Background
Under Menzies, Australia had limited conscription 
at the outbreak of WWII. Initially Australians were 
only conscripted to serve on the home front and 
in Australian protectorates. When Curtin took over 
as Prime Minister, Allied forces began to defeat the 
Japanese and the areas that conscripted soldiers could 
serve in were extended. 
A scarcity of goods in Australia during the war resulted 
in the introduction of rationing. Civilians were asked to 
help the war effort by living frugally.
Throughout WWII, censorship was exercised by both 
the Menzies and Curtin governments.
Starter activity
Explain to students that conscription means forcing a 
person to join a military force. Outline what a military 
force is – the army, navy or airforce. Ask students 
whether they would go to war, either voluntarily 
or if they were conscripted, and to give reasons for 
their answer. Remind students that attitudes towards 
war were different in 1939, and lead a discussion 
about these differences. Explain that in 1939, most 
Australians still had a thought of Britain as the ‘mother 
country’. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Conscription and conscientious 
objectors’, defines conscription and explores the 
reason for it in Australia during WWII. It also introduces 
students to the concept of conscientious objectors. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet ‘Conscription – yes 
or no?’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘Conscription and conscientious objectors’. 
Students will complete a definition activity and 
consider the pros and cons of conscription. 
	
Read the Resource sheet, ‘Rationing’, with the 
students. It provides information about why rationing 
was introduced in Australia during the war years, and 
how it worked. Make sure students understand the 
meaning of each term shown in bold.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘A week of rations’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘Rationing’. Students will complete comprehension 
questions and consider what foods their family would 
need to survive on food rations for one week. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Censorship’, provides 
information on censorship in Australia during 
WWII. Students will complete sentences about this 
information, and an exercise about gossiping.
Extension ideas
• 
Students could design a conscription poster for 
WWII. For ideas, they could research examples on 
the Internet. 
Objectives
• To understand the meaning of the word 
conscription
• To learn about conscription in Australia during 
WWII.
• To learn about rationing in Australia during 
WWII
• To learn about Australian censorship in WWII.
Prior knowledge
Students need to know that WWII was fought in 
Asia, as well as in Europe.

47
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Contribution and survival
 
Background
Labour shortages and a scarcity of commodities on 
the WWII home front resulted in civilians constantly 
finding ways to contribute to the war effort. Rationing 
was implemented in 1942 and austerity was promoted. 
Civilians found ways to stretch their rations; for 
example, many people grew their own vegetables and 
fabric from unwanted clothes was used to create new 
clothes. Advertising persuaded civilians to use less coal 
and electricity.
The Commonwealth and local governments 
encouraged recycling, and many young people took 
an active role in this process. Rubber, scrap metal and 
newspapers were collected. Investment in war bonds 
was also encouraged.
Starter activity
Write the words contribution and survival on the board. 
Ask students to brainstorm what these words mean. 
Write their suggestions on the board and then provide 
students with the following definitions.
Contribution is the giving of time, money or help to a 
common cause.
Survival is managing to continue to live or exist.
Discuss contribution and survival in terms of what they 
might have meant to Australian civilians during the 
war. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘How civilians helped with the 
war’, provides information about the ways that civilians 
contributed to the war effort. It also provides a primary 
source in the form of a photograph of the Ginger 
Meggs Salvage Corps. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Civilians during 
the war’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘How civilians helped with the war’. Students 
will answer comprehension questions, complete 
definitions and respond to a primary source.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Teenage perspectives’, 
provides an insight into the lives of two Australian 
teenagers during wartime. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Helping and 
surviving’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘Teenage perspectives’. Students will list ways 
a teenager could contribute to the war effort and 
identify statements as true or false. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Journal entry’, introduces the 
diary of Anne Frank. Students are asked to imagine 
that they are teenagers in WWII, and create a journal 
entry about a day in their imagined lives.
Extension ideas
• 
Students could research further information about 
the contribution of Australian civilians to the war 
effort, and present what they find as a multimedia 
report. Students could start their research with  
the website: 
	
www.ww2australia.gov.au/allin/warwork.html
• 
Students could read The Diary of Anne Frank.  
They could also research the story of how Anne’s 
diary came to be published. A useful website: 
	
www.annefrank.org
Objectives
• To understand that WWII created labour 
shortages on the home front
• To learn how Australian civilians contributed to 
the war effort
• To recognise survival and recycling strategies 
used on the home front
• To examine a primary source photo
Prior knowledge
Other than an awareness that many Australians 
were engaged in overseas warfare, students need 
no prior knowledge to complete these activities.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

53
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Indigenous involvement
 
Background
Prior to WWII, and when it began, Indigenous 
Australians were not officially allowed to enlist in 
military forces. The threat of Japanese invasion 
changed this. However, Indigenous members of 
Australian military forces generally were not paid the 
same amount as non-Indigenous members. Despite 
this, Torres Strait Islanders and Aboriginals made a 
significant contribution to WWII. Two well known 
Indigenous contributors were Leonard Waters and  
Reg Saunders.
Starter activity
Ask students to list the famous Indigenous people 
they know. Write the names on the board, and 
summarise why they are famous. Explain to students 
that Indigenous people contributed significantly to 
WWII by joining Australia’s military forces and helping 
on the home front.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Aboriginal and Torres Strait 
Islanders participation’, provides background 
information about Indigenous participation in WWII. 
It also introduces the Aboriginal poet Oodgeroo 
Noonuccal (also known as Kath Walker) who served in 
the Australian Women’s Army Service. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Remembering information’, 
provides a cloze exercise and comprehension 
questions about the information on the Resource 
sheet, ‘Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders 
participation’. You could challenge students to test 
their memory by completing the activities without 
referring to the Resource sheet.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Northern Territory Special 
Reconnaissance Unit (NTSRU)’, outlines the role of the 
NTSRU and provides a related map exercise. Students 
will need an atlas to complete this activity sheet.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Leonard Waters’, provides a 
profile of the first Indigenous Australian to become a 
fully qualified pilot. Students are asked to respond to 
this information and to a photograph of Waters. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Reginald Saunders’, provides 
profile of the first commissioned Indigenous soldier. 
Students are asked to respond to this information and 
to a photograph of Saunders graduation from the 
Officers’ Cadet Training Unit. 
Extension ideas
• 
Students could research Reginald Saunders and 
find out about his brother. Note that his brother 
Harry also fought in WWII and was killed on the 
Kokoda Trail. Students could start their research 
with the website: 
www.awm.gov.au/exhibitions/fiftyaustralians/ 
43.asp
• 
Have students research Oodgeroo Noonuccal 
(also known as Kath Walker), who is well known 
for her poetry and for her work in civil rights. 
Encourage students to find and read at least 
one of her poems. Students could also create a 
timeline showing important events in Oodgeroo’s 
life. Students could start their research with 
the websites below, or simply type ‘Oodgeroo 
Noonuccal’ into an Internet search engine. 
	
www.ict.griffith.edu.au/~davidt/redlandbay/
oodgeroo.htm 
	
www.library.uq.edu.au/fryer/treasures/yusuf/kath.
html
Objectives
• To explore the contribution of Indigenous 
Australians to WWII
• To learn about to two significant Indigenous 
people
• To examine primary source photos
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
59
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Australian women in the war
Background
During WWII, Australian women played a major 
role both on the home front and abroad. There was 
resistance to women taking on traditional male roles. 
However, necessity overcame this resistance. Women 
joined a number of organisations closely affiliated with 
the armed services.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what jobs the class thinks women and men 
should have in a war. Write the students’ ideas on the 
board and encourage them to give reasons for their 
views. Explain to the students that the roles of women 
and men in society were very different in that time, 
compared to today. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Women on the home front’, 
outlines some of the jobs women did during WWII. 
It also introduces the idea that the role of women 
in society changed dramatically at this time. Read 
the sheet with the students and make sure they 
understand the meaning of the terms shown in 
bold. Ask students if they think the poster would be 
effective for recruiting women, and to give reasons for 
their opinions.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Jobs done by Australian 
women’, asks students to compose a list of jobs 
performed by women during WWII. It also defines 
acronym and provides a table of related acronyms. To 
extend the activity, students could research one of the 
organisations listed in the table.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Looking at a poster and a 
photo’, asks students to respond to the recruitment 
poster on the Resource sheet, ‘Women on the home 
front’. It also provides a photo of women repairing a 
plane for students to respond to. 
	
In the Activity sheet ‘Australian women serving 
abroad’, students are provided with information about 
nurses serving abroad and the Australian Women’s 
Army Service. Students will answer questions about 
this information. Question 2 answers: a Australian,  
b drove, c service, d worked, e necessary, f people.
	
In the Activity sheet, ‘Letter to a husband’, students 
will read and respond to a wartime letter.
Extension ideas
• 
Have the students imagine that they are involved 
in WWII. Ask them to write a letter to a close friend 
or relative who is posted overseas for the war.
• 
Word building – write the words information, 
communication and organisation on the board. 
Explain to the students that these words are the 
noun forms of verbs. Work as a class to construct a 
verb/noun table like the one below. 
Verb
Noun
inform
information
communicate
communication
organise
organisation
regulate
regulation
negotiate
negotiation
navigate
navigation
Objectives
• To recognise the role of Australian women on 
the home front in WWII
• To recognise the role of Australian women 
abroad in WWII
• To develop skills in responding to primary 
documents
Prior knowledge
No prior knowledge is required for this unit.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Contributing causes
The Treaty of Versailles
Soon after World War I (WWI) ended, a number of world 
leaders met to officially end the war. This meeting was called 
the Paris Peace Conference. It was held at Versailles Palace, 
near Paris. One purpose of the conference was to make 
Germany pay war damages. The most powerful nations 
represented at this conference were Britain, France, the 
United States of America, Italy and Japan. William Hughes, 
the Australian Prime Minister, also attended. Germany was 
not invited. 
Germany believed the peace treaty would be based on 
a fourteen-point plan developed by Woodrow Wilson 
(President of the USA) aimed at keeping world peace. France 
thought this plan was not severe enough – they wanted 
Germany to accept blame for starting WWI. 
After much debate, the Treaty of 
Versailles was signed on the 28th of 
June, 1919. This treaty included a war 
guilt clause and Germany had to accept 
blame for starting WWI. Germany also 
had to pay millions of pounds to some 
Allied nations, especially France. 
The Treaty of Versailles demanded that:
•   Germany pay huge war reparations.
•   Germany restrict the growth of its 
military forces. 
•   Germany decrease its territory. 
How did Germany react to  
The Treaty of Versailles?
Many Germans felt that the Treaty of 
Versailles was too severe. The huge war 
reparations Germany had to pay meant 
Germany’s economy suffered. Extreme 
groups in Germany promised they 
could make Germany a better nation. 
The Nazi Party was formed in 1919 and 
Adolf Hitler became the party’s leader 
in 1921. He promised to overturn the 
losses Germany experienced as a result 
of the Treaty of Versailles. 
Allied nations at  
the end of WWI
• Australia 
• Britain 
• Canada
• France
• Italy
• Japan
• Russia
• United States of 
America

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
The Great Depression and insecurity
A depression is a severe slump in an economy. Businesses find it hard to make any profit 
and people lose their jobs. On 24th October, 1929, the New York stock market crashed.  
This marked the beginning of the Great Depression and it continued into the 1930s. 
The Great Depression spread to other countries. Some countries decided they needed more 
land to supply raw materials to help their industries survive. Japan invaded Manchuria in 
1931. Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935. Germany invaded parts of Eastern Europe. 
During the Great Depression there was very 
high unemployment, which created a feeling 
of insecurity (not being safe). Many people 
were poor. 
In some countries, people turned to leaders 
who promised to make their nations strong. 
These leaders built up their supplies of 
arms (weapons) and tried to take land that 
belonged to other nations. Adolf Hitler from 
Germany and Benito Mussolini from Italy  
were two such leaders. 
Resource sheet – Contributing causes
Policy of appeasement
In the1930s, France and Britain 
decided the Treaty of Versailles was 
too harsh on Germany. They followed a 
policy of appeasement (compromise 
in the hope of avoiding another war). 
In 1938, Germany, France, Britain and 
Italy signed the Munich Agreement, 
which agreed to Hitler’s claim that 
part of Czechoslovakia belonged to 
Germany. Neville Chamberlain, the 
British Prime Minister, believed Hitler 
would not claim any more territory 
but in March 1939 Hitler invaded all of 
Czechoslovakia. 
Some historians argue that the 
Great Depression contributed to 
the policy of appeasement because 
Allied nations were not in a financial 
position to stop Hitler’s imperialism. 
The financial losses caused by the 
Great Depression also meant that 
France and Britain did not put as 
much money into building up their 
supplies of weapons.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Adolf Hitler
Adolf Hitler gained political power by 
promising to improve the German economy 
and restore Germany to her former glory. 
Why people supported Hitler
Hitler was a charismatic leader. He could 
capture people’s imaginations and persuade 
people to believe in him. He was also a 
skilful orator. He could give inspiring 
speeches that attracted large crowds.
In 1921, Hitler became the leader of the Nazi 
party. He became the German Chancellor 
(head of the German government) in 1933. 
Once in power, Hitler banned all opposition. 
He used the secret police and the military to  
quash anyone who opposed him. He referred  
to his one-party government as the Third Reich.  
He called himself Führer, which is German for ‘the leader’. 
Hitler’s goals
Hitler aimed to establish a perfect, superior race. He believed real Germans descended 
from the Aryans. The Aryans were people with blonde hair and blue eyes. Hitler wanted to 
rid Germany of Jewish people because he thought they were inferior. He sent millions of 
Jewish and other non-Aryan people to concentration camps.
Hitler used propaganda to spread his beliefs. Propaganda is misleading or incorrect 
information that persuades people to believe what you want them to believe. Hitler used 
propaganda to promote his ideas about the perfect race and explain why millions of Jews 
and non-Aryan people should be persecuted.
In 1939 Hitler invaded Poland because he wanted more land for his expanding empire. It 
was this event that sparked WWII. 
Hitler was a dictator – he governed with absolute power.

Resource sheet – Totalitarianism and dictators
Benito Mussolini
Benito Mussolini was an Italian 
who dreamt of returning Italy to 
her ancient glory. He began the 
Italian Fascist Party and was  
its leader.
In 1922, King Victor Emmanuel of 
Italy appointed Mussolini as Italian 
Prime Minister. Mussolini was the 
youngest man ever to hold this 
position. Once in power, Mussolini 
quickly became a dictator.
Why many Italians  
supported Mussolini
After WWI, Italy was in chaos. Many Italians believed Mussolini could improve Italy’s 
economy and bring stability to Italy. To help solve the problem of unemployment, 
Mussolini started rebuilding Italy’s roads and public transport system which provided 
many jobs. Like Adolf Hitler, Mussolini had a charismatic personality. He was a brilliant 
public speaker.
Mussolini and the League of Nations
The League of Nations was established at the end of WWI. Its aim was to promote 
international cooperation between nations and keep peace. Mussolini ignored the 
League’s attempts to resolve Italy’s land claims in Abyssinia. Instead of accepting some 
Abyssinian land, Italy invaded Abyssinia in 1935. The League imposed trade sanctions on 
Italy because of this military action.  This meant that Italy could not easily import or export 
goods. However, these trade sanctions were not really enforced and Italy continued its 
expansion into parts of Africa.
Mussolini outlawed opposition
Mussolini did not tolerate people disagreeing with him or his fascist party. He used secret 
police and had strong military support. He even had his own military force called the 
Blackshirts. The Blackshirts murdered and tortured people who opposed Mussolini. Many 
people lived in fear of Mussolini’s dictatorship. Like Hitler, Mussolini was a ruthless leader.

after their last meeting, April 1943

Resource sheet – The rise of the Nazi Party
The National Socialist  
German Workers’ Party
The Nazi Party is the shortened name of the National Socialist German Workers’ Party. 
It was an extreme right-wing political party that began in 1919, with only fifty members. 
Adolf Hitler became the leader of the Nazi Party in 1921.
The Nazi Party claimed that the Weimar 
Republic (the German government) should 
not have signed the Treaty of Versailles. The 
Nazi Party gained popularity by blaming the 
Weimar Republic for Germany’s economic 
losses. Germany had very high levels of 
unemployment during the Great Depression. 
The Nazi Party promised that it could create 
more employment for German people.
In 1933, the Nazi Party was the largest party in 
the German parliament. By 1939 when WWII 
began, it had millions of supporters.
Crushing of opposition
Hitler insisted that people be loyal to him. He made every German soldier swear an oath 
of loyalty. Under Hitler’s leadership, the Nazi Party made Germany into a police state. 
Secret police were used to control people’s lives. Hitler used the SA (commonly known as 
Brownshirts), the SS (The Schutztaffel, meaning protective squadron) and the Gestapo to 
crush any opposition.
The Brownshirts were young unemployed men who beat and killed enemies of the Nazi 
Party. The SS was a powerful military group set up to protect Hitler. SS members either 
killed Hitler’s opponents or sent them to concentration camps. The Gestapo was the 
Nazi Party’s secret police force. The Gestapo had no respect for individual rights and sent 
thousands of people to concentration camps.
What was the Weimar Republic?
In 1919, a national assembly met in 
the German town of Weimar and 
formed a new German constitution. 
They wanted to form a democratic 
government for Germany. 
A German parliament called the 
Reichstag was established. Germans 
could now vote for their own 
representatives to govern them. 
This new democracy was named the 
Weimar Republic.

Nazi Youth
The Nazi Party believed that Germany’s future lay with its young people. German boys 
aged thirteen to eighteen were expected to join the Hitler Youth Group. Younger boys 
were expected to join a junior Nazi group. Teenage girls were expected to join the League 
of German Girls. A lot of physical training was given in these groups.
Both boys and girls were indoctrinated with Nazi propaganda. Parents who didn’t let 
their children join the Hitler Youth risked imprisonment.
What members of Nazi Youth groups were taught
• The Treaty of Versailles was totally unfair.
• Jews and other non-Aryans were inferior.
• An Aryan race would become the master race.
• Adolf Hitler would make Germany a powerful nation.
• Nazis would rule the world.
• Germany needed more Lebensraum (living space).
• How to use weapons.

Two different perspectives
Karl, 15-year-old 
German, 1934
Yesterday I joined Hitler’s Youth group. Mum didn’t want me to but 
Dad said he wasn’t going to risk prison. He said that Germany has 
suffered enough and that it looks like Hitler will stop us having to 
pay war debts. Anyway, I wanted to join. I want to wear a uniform 
and really push myself with physical training, go on special camps 
and make new friends. One day, I want to join the Nazi Party. I 
really like our Führer. He’s brilliant – a fantastic speaker. He’s going 
to make Germany the best country in the world. 
I used to love living in Germany but now I’m scared to leave 
our house. Whenever I go out I have to wear a Star of David 
badge. People shout at me and tell me I’m a dirty Jew. Dad 
says it’s getting too dangerous to live here. Hitler keeps giving 
speeches about how Jews are inferior. What really hurts is that 
most of my German friends won’t talk to me anymore. I really 
worry about Mum. Since her friends had their shop windows 
smashed, she won’t leave the house. I heard her telling Dad 
some of her friends don’t answer her phone calls. She thinks 
they’ve been sent to concentration camps.

Resource sheet – Outbreak of war  
and Australia’s response
1939 Invasion of Poland
In 1938 Neville Chamberlain, the British Prime 
Minister, signed a pact with Adolf Hitler called 
The Munich Agreement. It allowed Hitler to keep 
territory in Czechoslovakia, and Hitler claimed 
he would not take any more territory. 
In 1939, Germany signed the Nazi–Soviet Pact 
with the Soviet Union. Publicly, the pact stated 
that the two nations wouldn’t attack each other 
for ten years, and that the Soviet Union would 
exchange raw materials for manufactured 
German products. Secretly, the pact stated that 
Poland would be divided up between Germany 
and the Soviet Union.
Hitler was warned that if Germany  
broke the terms of the Munich 
Agreement and invaded Poland,  
Allied forces would declare war  
against Axis powers. 
Hitler ignored the Munich Agreement 
and invaded Poland on 1st September, 
1939. On 3rd September, 1939, Britain 
and France declared war on Germany. 
Polish military forces were not strong 
enough. On the 27th September, 1939, 
Poland surrendered to Germany. Hitler’s 
invasion of Poland was the immediate 
cause of WWII, and marks the beginning 
of WWII in Europe.
Major Allied 
forces at the 
start of WWII: 
• Britain
• France 
• Poland
Major Axis 
powers: 
• Germany
• Italy 
•Japan
Joining the Allied forces:
•  The Soviet Union joined in 1941, 
after Germany invaded Russia (a 
major Soviet Union country). 
•  The USA joined after the bombing 
of Pearl Harbour in 1941.
Australia’s reaction 
On the 3rd September, 1939, the Australian 
Prime Minister, Robert Menzies, made 
a famous speech. He announced that 
Australia was at war with Germany because 
Britain had declared war on Germany. 
Menzies said Germany was taking countries 
by force and it had to be stopped.
In 1939, Britain was viewed as ‘the mother 
country’ of Australia. Australia was part of 
the British Empire and many Australians 
believed that Australia should support 
Britain. However, not every Australian 
agreed with Menzies’ decision. Some 
thought the war was too far away for 
Australia to be involved.

Resource sheet – The Holocaust
Hitler’s propaganda against Jews
Propaganda is the spreading of false or misleading information to make people believe 
a particular thing. Under Adolf Hitler’s leadership, the Nazi Party used propaganda to 
convince Germans that Jews were an inferior race. This racism against Jews is called  
anti-Semitism.
The Nazi Party spread its anti-Semitic propaganda through radio broadcasts, newspapers, 
speeches, posters and films. Films showed Jews as subhuman creatures who were trying 
to destroy German society. For example, the film The Eternal Jew which was made in 1940 
tried to convince audiences that Jews were greedy and immoral. Other films portrayed 
Germans as a superior race. 
There were televisions in Germany from 1935. They were very big and only a few people 
had them. Hitler had plans to use television to show what perfect German couples were 
like and also what happened to Nazi traitors. He wanted to have televisions in public 
places so that everyone could watch them.
Nazi persecution of Jews
Persecution is constant cruelty towards an 
individual or a group of people.
●
●
Hitler forced Jews to wear a yellow Star 
of David, with the word ‘Jude’ (German for 
‘Jew’), on their clothes. The Star of David is 
a symbol of Jewish identity. Hitler wanted 
Jews to be clearly identified to everyone so 
that they could be imprisoned or killed.
●
●
A haunting example of Nazi persecution is Krystallnacht. In November, 1938,  
Nazi mobs bashed, arrested and murdered Jews in Germany and Austria.  
Jewish shops had their windows smashed and synagogues were destroyed.   
Over 90 Jewish people were murdered. Krystallnacht is also known as the  
‘Night of the Broken Glass’. 
●
●
Further persecution occurred when millions of Jews were separated from their 
families and sent to concentration and extermination camps.

Resource sheet – The Holocaust
‘The Final Solution’
‘The Final Solution’ is the name the Nazi Party gave to its policy of killing all European Jews. 
In history, there is often debate about the exact dates that things were decided.  
Historians are unsure of the exact date ‘The Final Solution’ policy was formed.  
However, it had two distinct stages. 
●
●
The first stage was in 1941 when German military forces invaded 
the Soviet Union. The military was closely followed by German 
task forces who shot any Jews they found. These special task forces 
decided it was too difficult to continue shooting Jews, especially 
women and children. This led to the second stage. 
●
●
The second stage of the ‘Final Solution’ began at a conference (the 
Wannsee Conference) held in 1942, when the Nazi Party decided to 
establish extermination camps. German industrialists were forced 
to build them, and Jews were sent to these death camps. The Jews 
were forced to work and then killed with  
poisonous gases.  
Gypsies, communists, Jehovah’s Witnesses, homosexuals, and disabled people were also 
sent to extermination camps. Historians have little data to indicate how many gypsies and 
disabled people were killed. Jews were sent to the larger death camps so there is more 
data about how many Jewish people were murdered.
What is data?
Data can be described as stored facts, information and statistics.  
Data can help historians work out things like: 
●
●
how many soldiers died during a war
●
●
how many people attended a conference
●
●
how many people live in a country.
It is important to remember that data can be altered and removed.  
This means that historians have to be careful when they study data.

Resource sheet – Concentration camps
What were Nazi concentration camps?
Between 1939 and 1945, Nazi Germany established many concentration camps. 
Concentration camps were prisons where people were made to work extremely hard. 
This is called forced labour. The camps were called concentration camps because the 
prisoners were concentrated in one place – that is, held together in one location. 
At first, concentration camps were used to imprison people who disagreed with Hitler 
and the Nazi Party. Jehovah’s Witnesses, disabled people and homosexuals were also 
imprisoned. However, throughout WWII, most of the prisoners were Jewish – millions were 
imprisoned and killed. This genocide of Jews is known as the Holocaust.
Many people in these camps died 
from starvation and exhaustion. 
Conditions were extremely harsh 
and only a few people survived. 
Nazi doctors carried out medical 
experiments in concentration 
camps. Prisoners were forced to let 
these doctors experiment on them.
Who guarded these camps?
These camps were run and guarded 
by Hitler’s SS. The SS stands for  
the German word ‘Schutztaffel’.  
It means a protective squadron.
Auschwitz concentration camp
Auschwitz, in Poland, was the largest concentration camp. Over a million people were 
killed there. Some were shot but most were killed with toxic gases. Auschwitz was used as 
a slave labour centre and an extermination centre. Bergen–Belsen and Buchenwald were 
the names of two smaller German concentration camps.
On 27th January, 1945, Soviet troops freed prisoners from the Auschwitz concentration 
camp. There is now a museum at Auschwitz in honour of the people who were 
imprisoned, tortured and killed there.

Resource sheet – The home front
Conscription and conscientious objectors
What is conscription?
Conscription means making a person enlist in a military force. Different countries have 
different rules about conscription. 
Conscription in Australia in World War II
1939:	 Men aged twenty years had to do military training. Young men were conscripted 
to defend Australia. This conscription was called home service and the troops 
could be sent anywhere in Australia. Troops could also be sent to Papua and New 
Guinea (PNG) because PNG was an Australian protectorate, which means PNG was 
protected by Australia.
1941:	 WWII was fought in the Pacific, as well as in Europe. Japan bombed Pearl Harbour 
in Hawaii in December 1941, and Australians fought with Allied nations to defend 
the Pacific from further Japanese attacks. 
1942:	 When Japan bombed Darwin on 19th February, 1942, the Australian government 
realised it had to make sure there were enough soldiers to protect the country. 
Eighteen-year-olds now had to sign up for military service. Australian troops in 
PNG helped prevent Japan from using PNG as a military base, from which it could 
have easily invaded Australia. 
1943:	 The law was changed to allow conscripted soldiers to fight beyond Australian 
shores to help Allied forces protect the Pacific from Japan.
Conscientious objectors
A conscientious objector is someone who 
objects to going to war on moral or religious 
grounds. Conscientious objectors could apply 
for an exemption from compulsory military 
service. An exemption means that you don’t 
have to follow the general rule. An exemption 
from compulsory military service means that 
you don’t have to serve in a military force.
There are different types of 
conscientious objectors. These include:
• 	pacifists, who believe it is wrong 
to engage in war in any way
• 	people who won’t carry  
weapons but will participate in 
non-combatant roles
• 	people who won’t go to war but 
will work as civilians to help the 
war effort.

Resource sheet – The home front
Rationing
A ration is a fixed allowance of a commodity. A commodity is a raw material or product, 
such as tea, sugar, spices and clothes. Rationing is the process of distributing (giving  
out) rations.
During WWII, Australians were encouraged to live frugally. This means they were asked 
to spend very little money and use fewer things. Clothing was rationed and some foods 
were too; for example, sugar, butter, meat and tea. Petrol, tobacco and alcohol were also 
rationed. Reasons for this rationing include: 
• a decrease in imported goods
• a decrease in the manufacturing of textiles and clothes
• a reduced labour force because many people were sent to the war.
How rationing worked
In Australia, food ration books 
containing food coupons were given 
out each year. There were special food 
coupons for pregnant women, people 
who were sick and for servicemen and 
servicewomen who were on leave. 
Sometimes different food coupons 
were used for different age groups. For 
example, in 1944, children less than 
nine years old didn’t receive tea rations. 
Children who were less than five years 
old had more coupons for eggs.
Clothing cards were also issued annually. These had coupons that could be torn off when 
someone wanted to buy an item of clothing. Pregnant women and people working in 
some industries received special clothing coupons. People could also swap their coupons. 
During this time of rationing, people had to make clothes last a long time, and also think 
of ways to make food go further. Even holidays were rationed – the Christmas and New 
Year holiday period was reduced to only three days.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
46
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Activity sheet – The home front
Censorship
Censorship is the official control of information. During WWII, the Australian government 
used censorship to control speeches, radio broadcasts, films, newspapers and images. 
Robert Menzies was the Prime Minister when the war started. The Menzies government 
set up a special department called the Department of Information to control what 
information about the war was reported to civilians. 
The letters that soldiers wrote to their friends and family were read by censors. 
Information that was thought to be dangerous was crossed out.
The Australian government claimed that censorship stopped important information from 
reaching the enemy. Censorship was also used to boost the morale of people at home. For 
example, when Darwin was bombed by Japanese forces in 1942, some details were not 
broadcast on the radio or printed in newspapers. This stopped people from panicking and 
led people to believe that the Australian government had things under control.

Gossip is idle talk, and can include the spreading of rumours. The Australian government 
told citizens not to gossip about WWII because they did not want people to panic. It was 
also important to make sure that people did not give information to the enemy. This was a 
type of censorship.
2	 Write three things that could have been gossiped about during WWII; for example, the 
bombing of Darwin.

Achieve!
Resource sheet – Contribution and survival
How civilians helped with the war
Many Australian men and women 
were in the armed services but others 
also contributed to the war effort. 
Civilians helped a lot on the home 
front. A civilian is a person who is not 
in the armed services.
In WWII there were labour shortages 
because so many men and women were 
overseas serving in the armed forces.  
Civilians made up this shortfall in labour.
Some ways civilians helped
• Helped build air-raid shelters
• Volunteered to help charities
• Volunteered their labour on farms
• Worked in factories
• Helped look after factory workers’ children
In WWII there were shortages of food, 
petrol and other commodities. This 
meant that civilians needed to think 
of ways to be thrifty. Being thrifty 
means finding ways to save money. The 
Australian government encouraged 
recycling. Some companies held 
competitions to see who could collect 
the most scrap metal, rubber and 
newspapers.
Some ways civilians were thrifty
• Used scraps of material to make  
new clothes.
• Grew their own vegetables
• Recycled newspapers
• Didn’t waste food
• Used less coal and electricity
The photo of the Ginger Meggs Salvage 
Corps and their billy cart was taken on 
16th April, 1943. The billy cart was used  
to collect things that could be recycled.  
It is a primary source because it was 
taken during the time of WWII.
Members of the Ginger Meggs Salvage Corps 
with their billy cart and salvage at the  
Raleigh Street State Primary School
Courtesy, Australian War Memorial 138617

50
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Resource sheet – Contribution and survival
Teenage perspectives 
A perspective is a way of looking at something. Below are two teenagers’ perspectives on 
life during WWII. 
Hi, I’m Alex. I’m fifteen years old. I live 
with my mum and two younger sisters. 
Dad’s off fighting somewhere in the 
Pacific. Mum still makes me go to school 
five days a week. After school, I work 
in our vegie plot. My sisters help me. 
We grow lettuce, beans, spinach and 
tomatoes, and we have chooks. Mum has 
a ration book with 112 coupons. She gets 
tea, butter and sugar and a little meat 
but that’s not enough to feed us all. Each 
week we swap eggs with our neighbour 
for lemons and nectarines. I also work 
as a volunteer on a farm on Saturdays, 
digging up potatoes. It’s hard work but 
Mum says it really helps the war effort. 
Things are a bit crowded in our house – 
a family from Darwin is staying with us. 
They were evacuated after the Japanese 
bombing.
I wish Dad would come home soon. I 
really miss him. Mum worries about him 
all the time. So do I, but I keep telling 
Mum that things will be ok.  
Hi there. I’m Sally. I’m fifteen years old. 
Dad died when I was three. I have an 
older brother, Hugo. He’s in Europe, 
working as a pilot with the RAAF. My 
older sister Vera is working with the 
Australian Army Nursing Service in 
Egypt. Her last letter said she’s really 
busy looking after injured soldiers. 
We haven’t heard from Hugo for ages.  
Mum’s worried that something‘s 
happened to him. I keep telling 
myself that he’s not dead. My friend 
said he might be in a prison camp in 
a place called Changhi. I hope not. I’ve 
heard terrible things about that place.
Mum says we have to be strong and 
do our bit for the war. Sometimes I 
walk for ages with my friends to find 
scrap metal and rubber for recycling. 
I also mind our neighbour’s kids 
when their mum goes to work in 
an ammunition factory. Mum works 
there too. Before the war, Mum never 
went out to work.

Journal entry
A journal is a place to record information about yourself. In journals, you can write about 
how you feel and the things you have done. In today’s world, you can have a paper journal 
or a digital journal. In WWII, people had paper journals. Anne Frank was a Jewish girl. She 
recorded her feelings and daily experiences when she and her family were forced into 
hiding from enemy forces. The Diary of Anne Frank is now a famous WWII diary.
+ 
Imagine you are a teenager during WWII. Write a journal entry about a day in your 
life – any day between 1939 and 1945. Start your journal with a sentence that 
introduces you. You can use the word bank to help.

Achieve!
Resource sheet – Indigenous involvement
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander 
participation
Before WWII began, Australia’s military forces had rules that usually stopped Indigenous 
Australians from enlisting. The government claimed this was because Aboriginals and 
Torres Strait Islanders were not of European descent. In 1939, some Indigenous men were 
allowed to join the armed forces because they claimed to belong to different nationalities.
Effects of the threat of Japanese invasion
From 1940, attitudes towards Indigenous people joining the military began to change. The 
Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour, the invasion of Singapore and the bombing of Darwin 
meant Australia needed more soldiers. The strong threat of Japanese invasion forced the 
military services to allow Indigenous people to enlist. 
The Australian government knew that the Japanese had contacts in Torres Strait, 
because many Japanese worked there on pearling boats. The government wanted to 
make sure that these contacts would not spy for Japan. In 1942, the Torres Strait Light 
Infantry Company was formed. Nearly all of its members were Torres Strait Islanders. They 
completed military training and worked very hard to defend the Torres Strait islands.
Indigenous women
Indigenous women also contributed to the war 
effort. They helped to raise money and organised 
parcels to send to soldiers overseas. Others 
enlisted in the Australian Women’s Army Service 
and the Australian Medical Women’s Army Service. 
The Aboriginal poet, Oodgeroo Noonuccal (also 
known as Kath Walker) is a famous Aboriginal who 
enlisted in the Australian Women’s Army Service.
c1942, Brisbane, Queensland. Studio portrait 
of Aboriginal servicewoman, Lance Corporal 
Kathleen Jean Mary (Kath) Walker, of Stradbroke 
Island, Qld, a communication worker with the 
Australian Women’s Army Service (AWAS).  
Courtesy, Australian War Memorial P01688.001

Northern Territory Special 
Reconnaissance Unit (NTSRU)
From 1941, a number of Indigenous men served overseas. However, the Northern Territory 
Reconnaissance Unit (NTSRU) is an example of Indigenous contribution to the war on 
the home front. This unit was a special task force made up of about fifty Yolngu people 
from East Arnhem Land. The unit’s role was to defend the northern Australian coastline 
from Japanese spies and from Japanese attack. Because Australia is an island, it was very 
important for the coastlines to be protected.

Leonard Waters
In 1942, Leonard Waters joined the Royal 
Australian Air Force (RAAF) and trained as a 
flight mechanic. He then trained as a pilot. 
Waters was the first Indigenous Australian to 
become a fully qualified pilot.
Waters was assigned to Squadron 78 and 
served in Dutch New Guinea and Indonesia. 
He bombed places where Japanese troops 
were posted. Waters flew a kittyhawk – a type 
of fighter plane – and called his plane  
‘Black Magic’. 
In 1945 at the age of 21, Waters became a 
Flight Sergeant. He was awarded war medals 
for his bravery and has a street named after 
him – Len Waters Street in Canberra.

you notice in the photo.
2	 Write two sentences about Leonard Waters. Remember that a sentence starts with a 
capital letter, ends with a full stop, and contains a verb (doing word). Remember to 
proof read your sentences for any mistakes.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Reginald Saunders
Reg Saunders was an 
Aboriginal who joined the 
Australian Imperial Force (AIF) 
in 1940. He started his overseas 
service in Libya and was then 
sent to Greece. His battalion 
survived heavy air attacks but 
had to withdraw.
The battalion was sent to Crete 
but the ship they travelled on, 
the Costa Rica, was bombed 
and sank. Some soldiers, 
including Reg, were picked up by a 
destroyer. In Crete, Reg and his battalion 
fought bravely against constant enemy 
air attacks. Allied troops had to leave 
Crete but some troops, including Reg’s, were left behind.  
Reg hid for a whole year in Crete and escaped in 1942.
Reg rejoined his battalion in New Guinea. His courage and strong leadership skills were 
noticed and he became the first commissioned Indigenous soldier. This means he was 
responsible for other soldiers and gave them orders. He became a platoon commander in 
New Guinea.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
60
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Women were usually paid 
less than men. During the war, 
many women had to make all 
the family decisions and deal 
with finances for the first time. 
They also had to cope with not 
knowing if family members who 
were at war were safe.
This poster is called ‘Join us in 
a victory job.’ It was made in 
1943. Its purpose is to persuade 
women to join organisations 
during WWII. It shows women in 
the WRANS, AWAS, WAAAF, AWLA and AAMWS,  
and a munitions worker. It is a recruitment poster. 
Voluntary work
Women did a lot of voluntary work, raising money for the war effort and sending clothes 
and food to soldiers overseas. One of the biggest voluntary organisations was the 
Australian Women’s Land Army (AWLA), established in 1942. Women aged between 18 and 
50 could join. The AWLA was a voluntary organisation because its members were civilians, 
not formally enlisted in the army. Women working in the AWLA were paid a small amount 
of money by farmers for jobs like planting crops, driving tractors and milking cows. Their 
efforts helped maintain Australia’s food supply.
Resource sheet – Australian women in the war
Women on the home front 
Before WWII, most Australian women worked at home, raising children and doing 
domestic chores. This work was unpaid. During the war (1939–45), many men left their 
jobs to fight in the war. These vacant jobs were filled by women.  
They included:
• working in factories, especially 
munitions factories
• working on farms
• driving army vehicles and ambulances
• working in telecommunications
• working as mechanics
• collecting intelligence information. 
Join us in a victory job – poster 
created for the Department of 
National Service, 1943
Courtesy, Australian War 
Memorial ARTV00332

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012

Jobs done by Australian women 
Making a list can help you remember information. For example, if you want to remember 
what to buy when you go shopping, you make a list.

An acronym is a word formed from the first letters of other words.  
For example, AWLA is an acronym for the Australian Women’s Land Army. 
2	 Fill in the missing vowels in the organisations listed in the table.

© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012

Activity sheet – Australian women in the war
Australian women serving abroad
During WWII, many Australian women served abroad (overseas). Nursing services were 
closely linked to the Australian navy, army and air force. Women served as nurses in the 
Middle East, Greece and Singapore. They worked under extremely difficult conditions and 
often put up with the same conditions as soldiers. When hospitals weren’t available, they 
worked in temporary medical wards. At times nurses went to the battlefields to care for 
wounded soldiers.
Many nurses were sent to Singapore because Singapore was an Allied base. When Japan 
invaded Singapore in 1942, sixty-five nurses were evacuated on the ship the Vyner Brooke. 
The Japanese bombed the ship and twelve nurses drowned. Other nurses were captured 
by the Japanese and shot. One nurse, Vivian Bullwinkel, pretended she was dead and 
survived. She lived to tell how brave here colleagues had been.
+ 
1	 Use the information above to help you complete the following information. 
a)	 During WWII, women served as nurses in the Middle East,                                 
and                                            .
b)	Nurses worked under                               	
	
	
	
	
	
	
     .
c)	 Many nurses were sent to                                        because it was an                                            .
d)	Japan invaded Singapore in                            .
The Australian Women’s Army Service (AWAS) was formed in 1941. Women in this 
service worked in many roles. They drove vehicles and worked as clerks, interpreters, 
typists and telegraph operators. Some also worked as guards. About 350 women in this 
service were sent overseas. Many people believed that women should not work outside of 
the home, but the AWAS was considered necessary because it allowed more men to take 
on combat roles.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 1
64
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Letter to a husband 
+ 
Read this letter from a woman to her husband who was fighting overseas in WWII.
Dear Joe,
I miss you so much and hope you are safe. The children miss you too. We were all 
so happy when we got your letter. I’ve started working in a munitions factory. A 
lot of women are now working outside of home because there just aren’t enough 
men left here to do all the jobs that need to be done. When I’m not at the factory, 
I’m trying to keep up with the housework. The children are doing more chores now, 
and they’re getting used to me being the boss of the house. You’d be so proud of 
them. Sally’s been knitting scarves to put in comfort parcels to send to soldiers who 
are far away from home. She’s hoping you get one of her scarves. Robbie’s joined a 
salvage corps. You should see some of the things he collects!
My darling, we only hear bits of news about Singapore and I can’t imagine what 
you’re going through. I want you to know that everything is fine here. I’m learning 
how to do new things every day.
Love always, 
Rosie xxx
PS – We’re growing our own vegies.
1	 Where has Rosie started working? 	 	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
2	 What reason does Rosie give for so many women working outside the home?
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
3	 Why do you think Rosie has to be ‘the boss of the house’?
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
4	 Imagine you are Rosie. Write three things you think would be important to tell Joe.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
5
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Background
Japan, Italy and Germany signed the Three Power 
Pact in 1940. This pact requested that Japan recognise 
Germany and Italy’s dominance in Europe, and that 
Germany and Italy recognise Japan’s mission to 
establish a Pacific empire. Pro-Nazi countries also 
supported this pact. The pact established Japan, Italy 
and Germany as Axis powers that fought against 
the major Allied powers of Britain, France, (with the 
exception of Vichy France), Russia (from 1941), and 
the United States (from 1941). Australia and other 
Commonwealth countries also fought with Allied 
powers.  
The war in the Pacific was sparked by the Japanese 
bombing of the US naval fleet at Pearl Harbour, 
Hawaii, on 7th December 1941. This surprise attack 
caused extensive damage. Over 2000 Americans 
were killed and over 1000 were wounded. On 8th 
December, US President Franklin Roosevelt requested 
that Congress recognise that the US was at war with 
Japan. Roosevelt’s request was successful and war was 
declared upon Japan.
The attack on Pearl Harbour was carried out in order to 
provide Japan with more time to acquire the resources, 
including coal, oil and iron, they needed to attack the 
Philippines, Burma (now Myanmar) and Malaya (now 
part of Malaysia.
Starter activity
Write the names of the major Axis and Allied powers 
on the board and ask students to copy them. Remind 
students that not all countries entered WWII at the 
same time. Then work with the students to use an atlas 
or the Internet to locate these places in the Pacific: 
• 
Darwin 
• 
Singapore 
• 
Pearl Harbour, Hawaii 
• 
Port Moresby, Papua and New Guinea 
• 
the Coral Sea.
This website would be helpful:  
www.combinedfleet.com/battles
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Activity sheet, ‘World War II in the Pacific’, provides 
a cloze activity which summarises significant events of 
the war in the Pacific. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘A major Japanese attack’, 
describes the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour. It also 
provides the main motivations for this attack. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Understanding the 
Pearl Harbour attack’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘A major Japanese attack’. Students will 
complete comprehension questions about the attack 
on Pearl Harbour. Strategy is also defined, and students 
consider the Japanese strategy behind the attack on 
Pearl Harbour.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Australia at war with Japan’, 
provides information about Curtin’s announcement 
of war with Japan and Australia’s shifting attitudes 
towards Britain and the United States. Students will 
answer related comprehension questions. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Singular and plural nouns’, 
provides rules and examples for forming plural nouns.  
Students will write their own examples. 
Extension ideas
• 
Students could research the Japanese invasion of 
Manchuria. This website would be helpful:
	
www.bbc.co.uk/history/worldwars/wwtwo/ 
japan_quest_empire_01.shtml 
Teacher’s notes – Attack on Pearl Harbour
Objectives
• To learn about the bombing of Pearl Harbour
• To learn about Australia’s response 
• To gain an understanding of how the bombing 
of Pearl Harbour led to American involvement 
in WWII
Prior knowledge
Students should be aware that WWII was fought 
on three main fronts: Europe, North Africa and the 
Pacific. Students should also know that Australia 
was already supporting Britain in the war.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

11
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Kokoda Trail
 
Background
Australian forces were sent to Kokoda to prevent 
Japanese forces from invading from the north coast to 
the south coast and capturing Port Moresby. Australia’s 
aim was to push the Japanese back and the only way 
this could be done was by defending the Kokoda Trail. 
The term ‘Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels’ refers to the indigenous 
Papua New Guineans who greatly assisted Australian 
soldiers on the Kokoda Trail.
Starter activity
Using a map of Papua and New Guinea, work with the 
students to locate Gona, Buna, Kokoda, Port Moresby, 
the Kokoda Trail and the Owen Stanley Range. Discuss 
what the map tells you about the terrain. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Stopping further Japanese 
invasion’, describes the location of the Kokoda Trail 
and outlines why Australian forces were sent there. 
Students will learn about the role of these forces and 
the conditions they endured. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Thinking about 
the Kokoda Trail’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Stopping further Japanese invasion’. 
Students will complete a missing letter exercise and 
a cloze exercise, and write their own sentences about 
the Kokoda Trail. 
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘A letter from a soldier’, 
students will complete a cloze exercise that provides 
a young soldier’s perspective on fighting along the 
Kokoda Trail. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels’, outlines 
who these ‘angels’ were and their role on the Kokoda 
Trail. Students will answer related comprehension 
questions. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Studying a photo from the 
Kokoda Trail’, asks students to examine a primary 
source photo. Students will use a word bank to help 
them construct a paragraph based on this photo.
Extension ideas
• Remind students that the Kokoda Trail is also known 
as the Kokoda Track. Have students visit the website:
	
http://kokoda.commemoration.gov.au 
	
Students could watch the short video about the 
Kokoda Trail, and then write down the names of two 
of the battles fought here. Possible answers: The 
Battle of Isurava, The Battle of Mission Ridge, The 
Battle of the Beachheads.
• Students could explore other aspects of the same 
website, such as the Veteran’s Accounts.  
Objectives
• To learn about the location of the Kokoda Trail
• To identify the role of Australian soldiers in 
Kokoda 
• To learn about the conditions endured on the 
Kokoda Trail
• To learn about Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
• To examine a primary source photo
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
17
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Survival on the battlefield
Background
Surviving on the battlefields of WWII was extremely 
difficult. Soldiers had to cope with harsh weather 
conditions, new weaponry and isolation. They also had 
to cope with the constant threat of disease. Survival 
methods varied. Some soldiers were well equipped, 
others froze and starved to death. A number of 
Australian soldiers survived because of help received 
from medical units. They were also helped by a 
strong sense of mateship. Intelligence gathering was 
responsible for saving a number of soldiers’ lives. Note 
that for this unit the word ‘soldiers’ has been used in its 
wider sense and includes navy and air force personnel 
as well as army soldiers.
Starter activity
Tell students that they are about to go on a long 
trip. On this trip they will need to think about food, 
accommodation, transport and communication. They 
will not have access to fast food chains, supermarkets 
or their family’s cooking. They will not have access to 
hotel accommodation or to Facebook, mobile phones 
or the internet. Ask students to draw up a table with 
the following headings: Food, Accommodation, 
Transport and Communication. Ask students to list 
items under each category.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Food’, provides an Australian 
soldier’s account of the kinds of foods soldiers 
survived on when serving in El Alamein. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Thinking about 
soldiers’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘Food’. Students will complete a true or false 
exercise and consider what they would place in a 
comfort parcel to send to soldiers in WWII.
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Some of the things 
soldiers had to cope with’, students will complete a 
cloze exercise that outlines the difficulties soldiers 
experienced. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Mateship’, explores the concept 
of mateship. Students will examine a source photo that 
presents a scene where soldiers display qualities of 
mateship. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Intelligence’, presents methods 
of gathering information in WWII. Students will 
consider differences in technology in WWII compared 
to today, and explain how intelligence helped soldiers 
to survive.
Extension ideas
• Have students use the Internet to find out three 
things about the Enigma machine – an electro-
mechanical device that Germany used to collect 
data. Useful websites:
	
russells.freeshell.org/enigma/
	
www.bbc.co.uk/history/topics/enigma
Objectives
• To inform students of some of the conditions 
on the battlefields
• To inform students of some of the ways soldiers 
survived on the battlefields
• To examine a primary source photo
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

23
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Australian prisoners of war
Background
During the course of World War II, thousands of Allied 
soldiers were captured and imprisoned as prisoners 
of war (POWs). Women, especially nurses, were also 
imprisoned. There were over 35 000 Australian POWs. 
Many were captured by the Japanese after the defeat 
of Allied forces in Singapore on 15th February, 1942. 
Others were imprisoned by German, Italian and Vichy 
French forces. 
Many prisoners were forced by their captors to work 
in horrendous conditions. The construction of the 
Thai–Burma railway, between 1942 and 1945, involved 
POWs working under inhumane conditions.  Australian 
POWs worked at both ends of this railway.
Conditions varied in prison camps but all POWs 
endured brutal conditions. Living conditions were 
cramped and unhygienic. Food was scarce and 
clothing was inadequate.  Diseases, including 
pneumonia, beriberi and malaria, were rampant.
Starter activity
Write ‘prisoners of war – POWs’ on the board. Explain 
that all nations involved in warfare take prisoners 
of war. Point out that POWs is the abbreviation for 
prisoners of war. 
Brainstorm what students think a prisoner of war is, 
and how a prisoner of war would be different from a 
prisoner serving a jail term because of a crime he or 
she committed.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘What are prisoners of war?’, 
explains this term and provides background 
information about POW camps in WWII. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘About prisoners of 
war’, students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘What are prisoners of war?’. Students will complete a 
word definition exercise and answer comprehension 
questions. 
	
On the Activity sheet, ‘Death marches’, students will 
complete a cloze exercise that outlines what a death 
march is, and learn about death marches in Borneo.  
	
The Activity sheet, ‘POW profile’, provides a 
brief profile of a real soldier. Students will compose 
questions they would like to ask him, and work with a 
partner to suggest the answer to one question. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Experiences of prisoners of war 
(POWs)’, provides an illustration of POWs in Changi. 
Students are asked to imagine that they are POWs and 
write a paragraph about a day in their lives.
Extension ideas
• Have students research Changi prisoner of war 
camp. Ask them to write down two things they find 
out about this POW camp. Students could work in 
small groups to create an oral or multimedia report 
to show the class. These websites will be helpful: 
	
http://www.historylearningsite.co.uk/prisoners_of_
war_WW2.htm
	
http://www.awm.gov.au/encyclopedia/pow/changi.
asp
Objectives
• To define the term prisoner of war.
• To learn about the experiences of Australian 
prisoners of war during World War II 
Prior knowledge
Students need to be aware of Australia’s allies 
and enemies during World War II. They should be 
familiar with the terms Allied and Axis powers.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!   History – World War II – Book 2
29
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – The Thai–Burma railway
Background
The Thai–Burma railway was built because the 
Japanese wanted to move their troops and supplies 
to Burma (now Myanmar) without the threat of 
Allied submarine attacks. Asian workers and POWs 
were forced to work on this railway. The conditions 
they worked under were shocking. International 
conventions governing the treatment of prisoners 
were ignored. Starvation, beatings and diseases led 
to the deaths of thousands of people. The railway 
became known as ‘the railway of death.’
Starter activity
Brainstorm why transport is important, especially 
during wartime. Ask students why, during war years, 
railways could be considered a safer method of 
transport than shipping. Record students’ ideas. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Railway of death’, explains 
why the Japanese wanted the railway built. It also 
describes who worked on it and the brutal conditions 
workers endured. Note that students will use the 
terms in bold to complete a definition exercise on the 
following Activity sheet. You could also discuss the 
meanings of these terms as you read the information 
with the students. Afterwards, you could revisit the 
discussion from the Starter activity and talk about how 
the information on this Resource sheet affects the 
students’ ideas.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Learning about 
words’, students will need to refer to the Resource 
sheet, ‘Railway of death’. Students will locate the words 
in bold on the Resource sheet and match them to their 
definitions. Students will also read about adjectives 
and complete a simple adjective exercise. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘A primary source – Australian 
POWs’, asks students to respond to a photo of 
prisoners laying track on the Thai–Burma railway. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Time capsule’, explains what a 
time capsule is and provides examples of items that 
could be placed in a time capsule. Students are asked 
to imagine being a POW working on the railway, and 
choose items that could be put inside a time capsule. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘A letter from a prisoner’, asks 
students to complete a letter from a POW who was 
working on the Thai–Burma railway, to his wife at 
home.
Extension ideas
• Many Australian POWs working on the Thai–Burma 
railway were captured after the fall of Singapore. 
	
Challenge students to use the Internet to find out:
	
– the date of the fall of Singapore
	
– what damage this event caused to Allied forces
	
– two other interesting facts about this event.
	
These websites will be useful:
	
www.ww2australia.gov.au/japadvance/ 
singapore.html 
	
www.historylearningsite.co.uk/ 
fall_of_singapore.htm
Objectives
• To learn about the construction of the  
Thai–Burma railway
• To learn about the treatment of workers on the 
Thai–Burma railway
• To study a primary source document
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.

them for inappropriate content and to ensure that
