35
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Three significant Australians
Background
Nancy Wake, Charles Mene and Sir Edward ‘Weary’ 
Dunlop were three Australians who made significant 
contributions to the war effort. 
	
The rebellious Nancy Wake was a key operator 
in the French Resistance movement. Wake inspired 
thousands and often risked her own life to help POWs 
and wounded Allied air personnel escape from the 
Nazis. 
	
Mene, an Indigenous soldier from the Torres Strait, 
served all the way through WWII, and on into the 
Korean War. 
	
Dunlop, an officer and a surgeon, protected and 
provided medical assistance to Australian POWs on 
a daily basis. This assistance was given despite the 
extremely harsh conditions he, and others, endured.
Starter activity
Brainstorm what it would be like being a doctor in a 
POW camp. Write students’ ideas on the board and 
ask them to identify the most significant difficulties 
they think a doctor would encounter. For example, a 
doctor might have had to amputate a leg and do his 
or her best to clean wounds with very limited medical 
supplies.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Nancy Wake’, provides information 
on Wake’s life and her role in the French Resistance. It 
also defines the French Resistance. A primary source in 
the form of a photo is also provided.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Recalling 
information’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Nancy Wake’. Students will answer 
questions about Wake and construct a sentence about 
to explain what courageous means. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Charles Mene’, provides 
background information on Mene’s role in WWII and 
raises the issue of differences in pay for Indigenous 
and non-Indigenous soldiers. You could work with 
students to locate the places mentioned on a world 
map. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop’, 
provides background information on Dunlop’s role 
as a POW surgeon, first in Changi and then on the 
Thai–Burma railway. You could show the students the 
photo of Australian POWs working on the Thai–Burma 
railway on the Activity sheet on page 32, and have 
them discuss what it tells them about the health of the 
POWs and their work conditions. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Thinking about 
Charles Mene and Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop’, students 
will need to refer to the two previous Resource sheets. 
Students will complete a definition exercise and 
comprehension questions. 
Extension ideas
• Students could imagine they are interviewing 
Nancy Wake, Charles Mene or Sir Edward ‘Weary’ 
Dunlop. Have them write five interview questions. 
Students could then use the Internet to try to find 
the answers to their questions. 
• Students could write a short report about Australia’s 
role in the Middle East Campaign in WWII. The 
following website would be useful.
	
www.anzacday.org.au/history/ww2/overview/ 
ww2-03.html
 
Objectives
• To learn about Charles Mene
• To learn about Sir Edward Weary Dunlop
• To learn about Nancy Wake
• To study a primary source document
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of conditions on 
the construction of the Thai–Burma railway would 
be useful.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

41
© Jennifer MacDonald and Blake Education 2012
Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Nuclear bombs
Background
On 6th August, 1945, the United States dropped a 
nuclear bomb on Hiroshima in order to end WWII in 
the East. However, Japan did not surrender. The US 
dropped a second bomb on the city of Nagasaki on 9th 
August. This resulted in Emperor Hirohito announcing 
Japan’s surrender.
Starter activity
Ask students what they think nuclear warfare is. Write 
their ideas on the board. Then provide students with 
the following definition: 
Nuclear warfare is when nuclear weapons are used in a 
war to inflict devastating damage on enemy nations. 
Point out to students that nuclear warfare has 
devastating consequences compared to traditional 
warfare. Use this idea to explore the meaning of the 
word ‘devastate’. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘Bombing of Hiroshima and 
Nagasaki’, provides students with information about 
the reasons for and the effects of the two atomic 
bombs. A primary source photo of a Japanese boy is 
also provided. You could discuss with the students 
whether or not they think the US should have used 
nuclear bombs on Japan.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Remembering 
information’, students will need to refer to the 
Resource sheet, ‘Bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki’. 
Students will complete comprehension questions and 
a definitions exercise and identify statements as true 
or false. To extend the activity, you could have students 
think about the young boy in the photo, and write 
a piece from the boy’s point of view, describing the 
bombing of Nagasaki and what it was like to grow up 
in Nagasaki in the years after the bombing.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘A special story – Sadako 
Sasaki’, presents a case study of a young Japanese girl 
who survived the initial bombing of Hiroshima, but 
developed and died from leukaemia due to radiation 
poisoning from the bomb.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Writing a letter’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, ‘A 
special story – Sadako Sasaki’. Students will  write a 
letter to Sadako Sasaki, using the supplied word bank 
to help. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Apostrophes’, provides some 
basic apostrophe rules for ownership and contractions, 
and related apostrophe exercises.
Extension ideas
• Explain to students that civilians are killed in wars, 
as well as soldiers. Divide students into pairs and ask 
them to think of arguments as to why or why not 
this is fair. 
• Have students use the Internet to find a pattern for 
an origami crane. An Internet search will provide a 
variety of options, or go to:
	
www.monkey.org/~aidan/origami/crane/
	
Encourage students to make the crane and 
experiment with other origami patterns. 
• Students could explore the website of the 
Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum, which provides 
further information about Sadako Sasaki, the effects 
of radiation and the peace declaration. Use the 
website below, or type ‘Hiroshima Peace Memorial’ 
into an Internet search. 
	
www.pcf.city.hiroshima.jp/index_e2.html
	
You could have students work in small groups to 
prepare a report about the museum and why it is 
important. 
Objectives
• To learn about the bombings of Hiroshima and 
Nagasaki
• To become familiar with the story of Sadako 
Sasaki
• To develop letter-writing skills
Prior knowledge
Some background knowledge of the war in the 
Pacific would be helpful but is not essential.
Suggested web addresses were functional at the 
time of publication but teachers should check 
them for inappropriate content and to ensure that 
they are still functional before use with students.

Achieve!
Teacher’s notes – Allied victory
 
 
Background
D Day stands for Deliverance Day. D Day occurred on 
6th June, 1944. This day was a turning point for Allied 
forces who, after four years of planning, successfully 
invaded the shores of Normandy. This invasion 
enabled Allied forces to later attack Germany from the 
east.
On 15th August, 1945, Emperor Hirohito accepted 
defeat and announced that Japan would surrender. 
This day became known as VP (Victory in the Pacific) 
Day.
Starter activity
Tell students that there are some days that change the 
course of history. Have the students write about a day 
that they think has changed their lives, and consider 
how their lives might have been different if this day 
had been different. Ask them to share this information 
with the class, if it’s not too personal.
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘D Day’, outlines the planning 
needed for this day to occur, and what happened on 
the day. It also points out the historical significance of 
D Day.  
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Writing a report’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, ‘D 
Day’. Students will write a simple report about D Day, 
covering a list of key points that are provided. Before 
students begin, discuss the difference between fact 
and opinion, and make sure students have a clear 
understanding of this difference. Students may also 
like to use the Internet or library to conduct further 
research for their reports. 
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Japan surrenders’, outlines 
factors that contributed to Japan’s weakening position 
in the war, and eventual surrender. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Definitions 
and comprehension’, students will need to refer 
to the Resource sheet, ‘Japan surrenders’. Students 
will unjumble words, match terms to definitions 
and answer comprehension questions. Answers to 
question 1: a) announced, b) limited, c) nuclear, d) 
surrender, e) forced, f) civilians.
	
The Activity sheet, ‘VP Day’, asks students to 
respond to a photo of VP Day celebrations in Bourke 
Street, Melbourne. 
Extension ideas
• Have students write a creative response to one of 
the following situations:
	
– Imagining they are a young soldier landing at 
Normandy on 6th June, 1944. Useful words: excited, 
scared, thousands, aircraft, battle, fast, comrade, 
beach, Allies, Germans. 
	
– Imagining they are in Melbourne on 15th August, 
1945, and have just heard the news about Japan’s 
surrender. Useful words: excited, joy, thousands, 
celebrate, dance, hope, future.
Objectives
• To learn about D Day
• To develop report writing skills
• To develop creative writing skills
• To learn about the surrender of Japan
• To learn about VP Day
• To study a primary source document
Prior knowledge
Students require some background knowledge of 
the progress of WWII for this unit.

Teacher’s notes – The Anzac spirit
Background
Anzac Day originally commemorated the Australian 
and New Zealand army corps’ battle at Gallipoli in 
WWI. Now Anzac Day is a time to pay respect to all 
Australian servicemen and servicewomen involved 
in wars. The spirit of Anzac Day is a concept that 
encompasses courage, determination and mateship.
Starter activity
Ask students if they know what a commemoration 
is. It may be helpful to point out the similarity to the 
word memory. Provide students with the following 
definition: 
A commemoration is a public ceremony which 
remembers and celebrates what people have done. 
Resource sheets and Activity sheets
The Resource sheet, ‘About Anzac Day’, provides 
background information on what Anzac stands for, 
why we remember Anzac Day and the spirit of Anzac 
Day. 
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Remembering 
the history of ANZACs’, students will need to refer to 
the Resource sheet, ‘About Anzac Day’. Students will 
complete a definition exercise, answer comprehension 
questions and construct a sentence about Anzac Day. 
Answers to question 2: a) remember, b) bravery,  
c) spirit, d) marches, e) people, f) served.
	
The Resource sheet, ‘Glorification or 
commemoration?’, provides two different teenagers’ 
perspectives on Anzac Day. Note that definitions of 
commemoration and glorification are provided on 
the following Activity sheet. You could share these 
definitions with the students before they read the 
Resource sheet.
	
To complete the Activity sheet, ‘Different opinions’, 
students will need to refer to the Resource sheet, 
‘Glorification or commemoration?’. Students will 
answer questions about the teenagers’ perspectives, 
and then give their own opinion. 
	
The Activity sheet, ‘Anzac Day symbols’, defines the 
word symbol. Students will complete a cloze exercise 
about symbols relevant to Anzac Day. 
Extension ideas
• Ask students to write five questions they can use to 
interview people about what they do on Anzac Day. 
Students could conduct the interviews with people 
of varying ages, and prepare a report outlining what 
they found out. 
Objectives
• To learn what Anzac stands for
• To understand the concept of commemoration
• To discover how the Anzac spirit lives on
Prior knowledge
Students need no prior knowledge for this unit.

Resource sheet – Attack on Pearl Harbour
A major Japanese attack
On 7th December, 1941, Japanese military forces bombed the United States (US) naval 
fleet at Pearl Harbour, on the island of Oahu in Hawaii. Hawaii is in the Pacific Ocean.
The Japanese made two strikes on Pearl Harbour. They used fighter planes,  
ships and submarines. 
This was a surprise attack that 
caused a lot of damage: 
• Over 2000 Americans were 
killed and over 1000 were 
wounded.
• Eighteen US warships were  
sunk or damaged. 
• Over 160 planes were 
destroyed. 
• Three US aircraft carriers were 
not attacked because they 
were out at sea. 
Japan did not attack the oil reserves that were located on the shores of Pearl Harbour.  
This allowed the Americans to rebuild their fleet.  
Why did Japan attack Pearl Harbour? 
Japan aimed to remove the US military from the Pacific. 
This would make it easier to attack countries in South 
East Asia. The bombing of Pearl Harbour was a strategy 
Japan used to try to stop the US from defending 
countries in the Pacific against Japanese attacks.
Japan was already at war with China. Because of this, 
the US, Holland and Britain had placed embargoes on 
trading oil and scrap iron with Japan. Japan needed these 
resources and was determined to get them by following 
a policy of imperialism. Japan wanted to expand its 
territory in the Pacific to get access to valuable resources.
Japanese fighter planes attacking 
Pearl Harbour, Hawaii, 1941
Significance of  
the attack on  
Pearl Harbour 
• This attack caused the 
United States to enter 
WWII. 
• It also resulted in a 
closer alliance between 
Australia and the US. 
Australia realised that 
it needed to look to 
the US for protection.

Activity sheet – Attack on Pearl Harbour
Australia at war with Japan
On 8th December 1941, one day after the attack on Pearl Harbour, the Australian Prime 
Minister, John Curtin, made an announcement. It was broadcast on ABC radio. Curtin 
announced that Australia was now at war with Japan. The next day, war was officially 
declared upon Japan.
A shift in thinking
A later speech by John Curtin, published in The Herald on 27th December, 1941, stressed 
the importance of co-operating with the United States to defeat the Japanese in the 
Pacific. Curtin’s speech is important because it shows that Australia was now not as 
closely linked with Britain. At the start of the war, Britain had been considered the ‘mother 
country’. By late 1941, attitudes had changed. Many people believed that Australia should 
look towards the United States for support.
+ Use the information above to answer the following questions. 
1	 Who was the Australian Prime Minister in 1941, after the attack on Pearl Harbour?
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
2	 Why was the Prime Minister’s speech in December 1941 important?
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
3	 What does the word co-operating mean?
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
4	 Explain the meaning of ‘mother country’.
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
5	 What was the shift in thinking for Australia?

Singular and plural nouns
Singular means one. Plural means more than one.  
A noun is a naming word, and a common noun names everyday things like uniform and 
shoe. For most common nouns, we add s to the end of the word to form the plural.
+

ship
Plural

ships
To form the plural of nouns that end in ch, x, sh, s, ss or x, we usually add es. 
2	 The table below shows two examples. Add two more examples of your own.

Plural

To form the plural of nouns that end in a consonant and y, we usually drop the y and  
add ies. Remember, a consonant is a letter that is not a vowel. The vowels are a e i o u.

Resource sheet – The Kokoda Trail
Stopping further Japanese invasion
Australian troops were sent to Papua New Guinea to prevent Japanese forces advancing 
towards Australia. Japan began occupying areas of Papua New Guinea from January 1942.  
In late July 1942, they landed forces in the north at Gona and Buna. They were preparing 
for an overland attack on the south coast 
city of Port Moresby. If Japan got control 
of Port Moresby and used it as a military 
base, attacking Australia would be easier. 
The Japanese would become more 
powerful in the Pacific.
The Kokoda Trail (or Kokoda Track) 
was the main route connecting Gona 
and Buna on the north coast with Port 
Moresby on the south coast. It went 
through steep mountains called the 
Owen Stanley Range. This mountain 
range made it difficult for Japanese 
forces to reach Port Moresby. 
What did Australian forces do?
Australian forces fought to protect Kokoda, a village 
on the Kokoda Trail. The Japanese wanted this 
village because it had an airfield. The Australians 
fought to prevent Japanese forces from getting any 
further along the trail but they nearly reached Port 
Moresby. Australian soldiers struggled until more 
soldiers were sent to help them. By early 1943, after 
close battles, the Japanese were defeated in New 
Guinea and were forced to withdraw. 
Conditions on the  
Kokoda Trail
The trail was often very 
narrow and soldiers had to 
battle their way through 
thick jungles and dangerous 
mountains. A number of 
Australian soldiers sent there 
were only 19 years old and 
had little military training. 
These soldiers navigated 
rivers and coped with 
swamps, mud and diseases.
The Kokoda Trail

A letter from a soldier
+ Use these words to complete the letter: the, and, it’s.
1942, Papua New Guinea
Dear Mum,
I miss you so much. Things are really hard here. We’re working our way along 
______ Kokoda Trail. Some people call it ______ ‘devil’s design‘ because 
______ a kind of hell on earth. It’s very dense ______ steep. There’s so 
much mud ______ I pull off at least five leeches a day. The wretched things 
somehow manage to crawl inside my boots. It’s really hard to keep things dry 
here but I remember what you told me about trying to keep my socks dry.  
I try to wash them every night ______ hang them on a branch. A lot of 
______ guys have come down with diarrhoea.  Some have caught typhoid. 
A few soldiers in my division have caught malaria. Mum, I don’t want you to 
worry ______ I want you to know I’m okay. You know me, a real survivor.  
I think being only nineteen helps because I’m fitter than some of ______ 
older soldiers. So far, I haven’t caught any diseases. There are these natives 
here who help us make our way along ______ track. They’re called Fuzzy 
Wuzzy Angels. They even help carry injured soldiers. Better finish this now 
because ______ getting dark. Sometimes there’s hardly any light here 
because ______ jungle is so thick. That’s what I hate most Mum – the 
darkness. I hear all these really weird noises ______ worry that ______  
Japs are about to attack us. I don’t tell anyone else how scared I am but  
I remember that you’re proud of me ______ that really helps.
Love always, 
Tim xxx

Activity sheet – The Kokoda Trail
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels is the name given to indigenous Papua and New Guineans who 
greatly assisted Australian forces on the Kokoda Trail. They were called Fuzzy Wuzzy 
Angels because of their frizzy hair and because they helped Australian soldiers. 
What did Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels do?
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels carried ammunition and 
supplies to Australian military forces.  Their 
loads were about 40 kilograms. Fuzzy Wuzzy 
Angels also often helped Australian soldiers 
carry their heavy packs.
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels carried wounded 
Australian soldiers on stretchers along the 
Kokoda Trail over very rough ground to try to 
get medical help. 
• Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels knew a lot about the 
local landscape and gave Australians valuable 
information. They also worked as scouts 
because they knew the Papua New Guinea 
landscape so well.
1	 Who are the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
2	 What were three things the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels did?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
3	 What does the word volunteered mean?
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
4	 Was the treatment of Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels always fair? Explain your answer.
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
 
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
	
Treatment of  
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels
Many more Australians would 
have died without the help of 
Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels but they 
were not always treated well. At 
first they had volunteered but 
authorities made it very difficult 
for them to leave the Australian 
army. They were not paid equal 
rates and there were times when 
they were not given enough food.

Resource sheet – Survival on the battlefield
Food
The food Australian soldiers ate during WWII depended on where they were located and 
the climate they were in. However, there were some basic foods that were issued to all 
soldiers. These foods needed to last a long time and be easy to transport.     
Hi, I’m Tony. It’s 1942. I’m an Australian soldier based in El Alamein, Egypt. It’s really 
hard to get fresh food here and the food we do get is rationed. I’m eating my dinner 
– bully beef, again. It’s canned corn beef and I’m sick of it. Then I’ll have a biscuit 
and cup of billy tea with some sweetened condensed milk. Luckily, I still have my 
enamel mug. 
Sometimes we get to eat stew. It’s made in an army cookhouse and put in this 
metal pot called a Dixie, and brought to us in a jeep. Problem is we only get food 
from the cookhouse when things are quiet. My mate Max tried turning some bully 
beef into rissoles. They tasted disgusting. 
I really miss my wife’s cooking. She makes the best Sunday roast. Can’t wait to get 
back to Australia. Too many flies here. This morning I swallowed a fly and I hate 
it when they get up my nostrils. The sand – so much sand. It gets into everything. 
Sometimes I get Weet-Bix for breakfast but sand gets into that too. Sometimes we 
get canned cheese and the sand even gets into that. 
The other day a group of us found a fig tree. I didn’t like figs back in Australia but 
now I love them. It’s so hard to get fresh fruit here. We have to be really careful with 
water. It’s rationed to two pints a day. Can’t use it to wash clothes, only to drink and 
believe me – you get really thirsty here.

soap, books, warm socks and other clothing.

Some of the things soldiers coped with
To cope means to deal with. In WWII, soldiers had to cope with many things.

__ __ __ __ __ __ __ of time. Mobile phones didn’t exist in WWII and 
soldiers often didn’t hear from their families for __ __ __ __ __ __. 
Women who worked as nurses, translators and telecommunication

Extreme climates

Soldiers in the Pacific had to cope with extremely __ __ __  weather  
and humidity, and monsoonal rains. Soldiers in Northern Africa had

Health
Very cold and very hot __ __ __ __ __ __ __ resulted in soldiers

pneumonia. In hot, humid weather, soldiers had to cope with fungal

Soldiers were also injured in battle. Many suffered from  
__ __ __ __ __ __ __ wounds.
New weaponry

Activity sheet – Survival on the battlefield
Intelligence
Intelligence and secret communication helped soldiers survive in the war. 
In WWII, technology wasn’t as advanced as it is today. Methods of intelligence included 
aerial reconnaissance (using aircraft to collect information about enemy forces), espionage 
(using spies), the use of radar, and the use of radio operators and decoding machines. 
Intelligence officers collected information about enemy forces. There were two main ways 
this was done.
• Radio (wireless) operators would record what they heard on paper. Each country used 
their own codes and intelligence officers would try to crack these codes. US intelligence 
broke Japanese naval codes and found out a lot of information about Japanese 
movements in the Coral Sea. This information helped the Allies win the Battle of the 
Coral Sea in May 1942. If the Japanese had won this battle, they could have captured 
New Guinea. Australia would have been open to a Japanese attack.
• In WWII there were many spies. A spy secretly collects information about an enemy. 
Donald and Peter Field were two Australian spies sent to New Guinea to gather 
information about Japanese forces. They worked as signalman and intercepted enemy 
messages from Japan. They were sworn to secrecy about their work for 60 years. 
+ 1	 List three methods of communication used in WWII, and three used today.
Used in WWII
Used today
2	 Describe one modern way a country could find out about an enemy’s next move.

Resource sheet – Australian prisoners of war
What are prisoners of war?
In all wars, people fighting on enemy sides are captured and held as prisoners. They are 
called prisoners of war or POWs. In World War II, over 35 000 Australians became POWs.
Many Australian POWs were captured by the Japanese after the fall of Singapore on 15th 
February, 1942. These POWs were imprisoned in camps in South East Asia. Other soldiers 
were imprisoned in camps in Austria, Germany and Poland. 
Life in prisoner of war camps
Surviving in these camps was extremely 
difficult. Conditions varied between camps 
but all POWs endured harsh conditions. 
Space was cramped, there was little food and 
clothing was inadequate. 
Many POWs were forced to work as slave 
labour for their captors. Some prisoners were 
treated brutally and had to work 12 to 16 
hours each day. Many prisoners were forced 
to work in freezing conditions. Others had to 
work in dense, humid jungles. 
Disease was common in all POW camps. 
These diseases included beriberi, malaria, 
cholera and dysentery.
What POWs were fed depended on which 
prison they were in. POWs in Changi had a 
better diet than POWs working on the  
Thai–Burma Railway. 
POWs in Poland and USSR often starved, but 
POWs in Germany were treated better than 
those in Asian prisons.
The Thai–Burma railway was one 
example of slave labour. Many POWs 
captured in Singapore by the Japanese 
were sent to work on a railway to 
connect Thailand with Burma.  
It became known as ‘The Railway  
of Death’. 
POWs there were rarely given anything 
to eat other than rice and gruel.  
The Red Cross sent these POWs food 
parcels but these were usually stolen.
Changi was the largest Japanese 
prisoner of war camp. It was located in 
Singapore and held approximately  
15 000 prisoners.
Changi POWs were given small 
amounts of rice, meat and flour, and 
smaller amounts of vegetables, milk, 
sugar, salt, tea and cooking oil. This 
changed in 1942, when prisoners were 
told they had to get their own food, 
except for rice. Changi POWs were 
allowed to have vegetable gardens.

POW profile
+ Read the profile of an Australian prisoner of war. 
Sergeant Rupert Ingram Petchell
Sergeant Rupert Ingram Petchell was a soldier in the 2/15 Field Regiment of the 
Australian Imperial Force. He was sent to Singapore in 1941 and captured by the 
Japanese. Sergeant Petchell was then sent to Changi prison camp. A year later 
he was sent to Thailand and forced to work on the Thai–Burma railway. Here he 
witnessed the deaths of many of his fellow soldiers. 
Sergeant Petchell suffered from beriberi, dysentery and cholera during his 
imprisonment but somehow he managed to survive the horrendous conditions. 
At times he ate grass so that he did not starve. When Sergeant Petchell returned 
to Australia, he weighed just 47 kilograms. He died in 1968. He was 62.
1	 Imagine Sergeant Petchell is still alive. Write four questions you would like to ask him.
2	 Read one of your questions to a partner. How does your partner think Sergeant Petchell 
would have answered your question?

Resource sheet – The Thai–Burma railway
Railway of death
The Japanese invaded Burma (now 
Myanmar) in 1942. They decided to  
build a railway between Thailand 
and Burma to make it easier to move 
troops and supplies. Using a railway 
was safer than shipping by sea, due 
to the possibility of attack from Allied 
submarines.  
The Thai–Burma railway was built 
between 1942 and 1945. It was 
approximately 415 kilometres long.
The people who constructed 
the railway worked under terrible 
conditions. It became known as ‘the 
railway of death’.
Diseases
Workers suffered from  many 
severe diseases, including beriberi, 
dysentery, cholera and malaria. 
They also suffered from ulcers and 
dehydration.
Working conditions
Workers were treated as slaves. POWs were 
forced to walk over 300 kilometres just to 
reach the railway site. POWs who couldn’t 
walk that distance were shot or left to die in 
the jungle. Food was inadequate and often 
rotten. Clothing was scarce. Men usually 
had no shoes and worked with no shirts. The 
weather was humid and workers had to cope 
with monsoonal rains.
Workers had to carry heavy loads and were 
given little time to rest. They were often 
beaten. Even sick people were forced to work.
Who worked on it? 
Thousands of Asian labourers and 
Allied prisoners of war (POWs) 
were forced to work on this 
railway. Many of the POWs had 
been captured in Singapore. Over 
2 600 Australian POWs died there.

Nancy Wake 
Nancy Wake moved from New Zealand to 
Australia when she was a toddler. She grew up in 
Sydney and left home at 16. When she was in her 
early twenties, Nancy left Australia for Paris where 
she worked as a journalist. 
In 1933, Nancy visited Vienna and saw how 
the Nazi Party treated Jews. Disgusted by this 
treatment, she decided to do anything she could 
to help those persecuted by Nazis. In 1939, Nancy 
married Henri Fiocca, a wealthy French man.  
In that same year, Germany invaded Poland.  
Nancy joined the French Resistance.  
Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
What was the French Resistance?
The French Resistance was an underground 
organisation that worked against the Germans 
after they occupied parts of France. The main 
aim of the Resistance was to weaken the 
German army so that Allied forces could win. 
The Resistance provided intelligence reports 
to Allied forces and killed German soldiers. 
They also helped many wounded soldiers and 
prisoners of war escape. 
Why is Nancy Wake 
remembered?
Nancy Wake was a courageous 
woman who helped save over 
a thousand lives. She delivered 
weapons and supplies to 
resistance workers. Once she rode 
a bicycle hundreds of kilometres 
in three days to find a radio 
operator. In 2004, Nancy received 
Australia’s highest civilian honour 
– the Companion of the Order of 
Australia. She died in 2011.
1945 studio portrait of Nancy Wake. 
Courtesy, Australian War Memorial 
P00885.001
The Germans tried to catch Nancy. Once she 
was caught but released before the Gestapo 
discovered her true identity. Nancy fled to 
England and convinced the British government 
to train her as a spy. She was dropped back into 
France and worked with the Resistance in the 
French mountains. The Gestapo called Nancy ‘the 
white mouse’ because they couldn’t catch her.

Charles Mene
Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders participated in WWII. Charles Mene was from a  
pearling family on Mabuiag Island.  
Although there was opposition to Indigenous 
Australians joining the Australian militia 
(Australian Army Forces), Mene managed to 
enlist on 4th September 1939, just one day 
after Prime Minister Menzies announced that 
Australia was at war with Germany. 
Mene originally served with the Wireless 
Guard on Thursday Island. Thursday Island 
became a military headquarters in WWII and 
served as a base for Australian and American 
military forces. Mene completed further 
military training in Ingleburn, near Sydney. 
In 1940 Mene was sent to the Middle East and joined 
the Syrian campaign. 
Mene survived fierce fighting as the Allies tried to 
prevent German forces from gaining control of eastern 
Mediterranean areas. Mene also fought with Allied 
forces in Tripoli, where they tried to prevent an Axis 
invasion of Egypt.
Mene then served in Papua New Guinea. He fought 
Japanese forces on the Kokoda Trail and survived 
horrific conditions – 111 men from Mene’s unit lost 
their lives. 
After Japan surrendered, Mene joined the Australian 
contingent of the British Occupation Force of Japan. 
He later served in the Korean War. 
Mene was awarded a military medal for the bravery 
and leadership he displayed.
Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
Paying Indigenous 
soldiers
When Charles Mene joined 
the militia, Indigenous 
soldiers were not paid the 
same amount of money as 
non-Indigenous soldiers. 
Mene and other Indigenous 
soldiers still chose to fight for 
their country. They showed 
other Australians that their 
contribution to defending 
Australia was just as valuable 
as the contribution of other 
soldiers.

Resource sheet – Three significant Australians
Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop
Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop was an Australian surgeon. In 1939 he joined the Australian 
Army Medical Corps. Dunlop was sent to Israel, Egypt and Greece.  He also worked at 
Tobruk and was then sent to Java, in Indonesia.
In March 1942, the hospital in Indonesia where Dunlop worked was captured by the 
Japanese. Dunlop was made a prisoner of war (POW). At first he was sent to Changi.  
Later he was sent to a prison camp in Thailand.
Conditions in the Thai camp were very harsh. The Japanese forced the POWs to work  
on the Thai–Burma railway. The prisoners were weak and didn’t have the right tools to 
build a railway.
What did Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop do?
• Dunlop constantly protected other prisoners. 
• Prisoners often suffered from diseases such as malaria and beriberi. Dunlop did his best 
to keep sick prisoners alive, but he had limited medical supplies. 
• Dunlop operated on wounded prisoners. Often, the only light he had was from  
kerosene lamps.
• As an army medical officer, Dunlop decided which prisoners were fit enough to work. 
Why is Sir Edward ‘Weary’ Dunlop remembered?
Dunlop is remembered because he was a 
respected officer, and a talented surgeon 
who showed great courage. An example 
of Dunlop’s courage was his saving of the 
life of another POW called Bill Griffiths. 
The Japanese were going to kill Griffiths 
but Dunlop stood in front of the Japanese 
bayonets and refused to move until the 
Japanese promised not to kill him.
Dunlop was knighted in 1969. Over ten 
thousand people attended his state funeral 
in 1993. 
Weary?
Sir Edward always worked extremely 
hard. The nickname ‘Weary’ comes from 
a play on words. ‘Dunlop’, Sir Edward’s 
surname, is also a brand of car tyres.
‘Tyre’ sounds like ‘tire’, meaning 
‘needing to rest’. Weary also means 
tired, or needing to rest. 
This is an example of traditional 
Australian humour.

Bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Hiroshima
On 6th August 1945, the United States dropped a nuclear bomb on the Japanese city of 
Hiroshima. This bomb, called ‘little boy’, was made from uranium. The US thought it would 
make Japan surrender and end the war in the East.
What did the ‘little boy’ bomb do?
• Caused many fires – from the intense heat and 
winds from the blast
• Destroyed two thirds of Hiroshima – nearly every  
building within thirteen square kilometres
• Killed approximately 70 000 people, and 
thousands more people died later from the  
effects of radiation
Japan refused to surrender so the US decided to  
bomb another Japanese city. 
Nagasaki
The US wanted to bomb Kokura, but bad weather 
led to a change of plans. The ‘fat man’, a plutonium 
bomb, was dropped on Nagasaki on 9th August 1945. 
Nagasaki was a Japanese shipbuilding city and an 
important military port. It had already been bombed 
five times. 
What did the ‘fat man’ bomb do?
This bomb also caused much destruction, although 
the waterways and hills protected some of the city. 
Many people died and others suffered horrific burns. 
Many also died later from the effects of radiation, 
which cause cancer, blood disorders, infertility and 
genetic disorders. 
Emperor Hirohito announced Japan’s surrender  
on 15th August, 1945.

A special story – Sadako Sasaki
This is a special story about a young Japanese girl, Sadako Sasaki, and an origami crane. 
• A crane is a bird. 
• Origami is the Japanese art of folding paper into shapes.  
Sadako Sasaki was two years old when the nuclear bomb was dropped 
on Hiroshima in 1945. Sadako survived the bombing but in 1954, she 
developed lumps on her neck and behind her ears. Doctors discovered 
Sadako had leukaemia, a kind of cancer. This cancer was a result of 
radiation poisoning from the bomb.
When she was in hospital, Sadako heard a Japanese legend which 
claimed that anyone who made a thousand paper cranes would be 
granted a wish. 
In one version of the story, Sadako made 644 cranes before she died. 
Her friends and family made another 356 cranes so that Sadako’s wish 
for peace all over the world might come true one day. 
In another version of the story, Sadako finished her 1 000 cranes before 
she died.
Sadako died in 1955. She was only 12 years old. Sadako’s wish inspired 
people to raise money to build a peace memorial, called the Hiroshima 
Peace Memorial. The memorial was completed in 1958. It has a statue of 
Sadako holding a golden crane. These words are written on the statue: 
This is our cry 
This is our prayer 
Peace in the world
Now, in memory of Sadako, people all over the world make paper 
cranes to try to bring peace to the world.

Apostrophes
An apostrophe looks like this: ’ 
An apostrophe is a punctuation mark that can be used to show ownership – that is, that 
something belongs to a person or thing. For example:
• the bomb’s blast – the blast belongs to the bomb
• America’s bomb – the bomb belongs to America
• Sadako’s wish – the wish belongs to Sadako
+ 1	 Put in the missing apostrophe in each sentence.
a)	 In WWII, soldiers letters were very important for their families.
b)	Sadako Sakasis wish was for worldwide peace.
c)	 Many of Hiroshimas buildings were destroyed by ‘little boy’.
d)	Nuclear warfares destruction is severe.
Apostrophes are also used in contractions to show that words have been joined. For 
example:
• don’t (do not)
• I’d (I had)
• won’t (will not)
• you’re (you are)
2	 Circle the contractions. Then complete the words that make up each contraction.
a)	 Japan didn’t surrender after Hiroshima was bombed. (did ____)
b)	Sadako decided she’d make 1000 cranes. (____ would)
c)	 I’ll visit the peace memorial. (__ will)
There is an exception to the apostrophe rule – it’s and its. 
• It’s stands for ‘it is’. For example: It’s a tragedy or it’s raining or it’s Tuesday. 
• Its shows ownership. For example: The cat drank its milk or Its destruction was terrible.
3	 Write two sentences about WWII that contain apostrophes.  
Try to include contractions and apostrophes showing ownership.

D Day
D Day took place on 6th June, 1944,  
in Normandy, France.
What does D Day stand for?
D Day stands for Deliverance Day,  
and is also known as the invasion of  
Normandy. The campaign behind  
D Day was called ‘Operation  
Overlord’. It took over four years of  
careful planning. US General Dwight  
Eisenhower was the supreme Allied  
commander of this operation.
What happened on D Day?
• On D Day, over 160 000 Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy. 
• Thousands of ships and aircraft were used. 
• US forces landed first, and were soon followed by other Allied troops. 
• There was intense fighting between the Allies and Germans. 
• The Allies defeated German forces.
False radio messages
The Allies had tricked the Germans into 
thinking they were going to land at 
Calais, which was 400 km away from their 
actual landing area. The British created 
false radio messages and even built fake 
army camps to make this trick work. 
The British called this false information 
Operation Fortitude. Operation Fortitude 
worked so well that Rommel, the 
commander of German forces in France, 
had returned to Germany to celebrate  
his wife’s birthday.
Resource sheet – Allied victory
What is the significance of D Day?
D day was one of the most important days 
of WWII because it marks the beginning 
of the end of Nazi control of Europe. Once 
Allied forces were in Normandy, they 
installed a pipeline that carried 172 million 
gallons of fuel across the English Channel, 
from the UK to France. This was called 
Operation Pluto. Pluto stands for ‘pipe line 
under the ocean’. This pipeline provided 
the fuel for Allied forces to free France and 
invade Germany from the west.

Resource sheet – Allied victory
Japan surrenders
Japanese soldiers believed they should fight for their Emperor and country until they died, 
rather than surrender. Japanese pilots would commit suicide by flying aircraft carrying 
explosive missiles and crashing them into Allied ships. This was called kamikaze.  
What changed?
Japanese resources were running 
dangerously low. Japan no longer 
had oil supplies and only had limited 
supplies of steel and rubber. Many 
Japanese people were also suffering 
from starvation. 
Japan was losing battles in the Pacific. 
The island of Iwo Jima, approximately 
1200 kilometres south of Tokyo, was 
captured by the Allies in February 
1945. The island of Okinawa was 
captured in June 1945. 
The bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
The US dropped two nuclear bombs on Japan. The first one was dropped at Hiroshima on 
6th August, 1945. Japan would not surrender until after the second bomb was dropped on 
the city of Nagasaki. Thousands of civilians died from these bombings.
Soviet–Japanese conflict of 1945
On 9th August, 1945, Soviet forces invaded Manchuria and defeated Japan’s Kwantung 
Army. Some historians argue that this is what forced the Japanese to surrender.
Surrender
Emperor Hirohito announced Japan’s surrender on 15th August, 1945. On 2nd September, 
1945, Japan signed formal surrender documents. This signing took place aboard the 
Missouri, a US battleship. The Japanese surrender officially ended WWII.

Resource sheet – The Anzac spirit
About Anzac Day
What does Anzac stand for?
ANZAC stands for the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps. During WWI, on 25th April, 
1915, Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli, in Turkey. The Anzacs dug 
trenches and fought Turkish troops for months. Many of the Anzacs were very young. Even 
though the Anzacs were defeated by Turkish forces, they will always be remembered. 
Who do we remember on Anzac Day?
Even though the original Anzacs fought in WWI, on Anzac Day we remember all the brave 
men and women who have served in wars and peacekeeping operations for Australia. We 
remember people who fought in WWI, WWII, The Korean War, the Vietnam War, the War in 
Iraq and the war in Afghanistan.
Anzac Day is held each year on the 25th April.
How do we remember Anzac Day?
The main way people remember Anzac Day is by going to, or watching an Anzac Day 
march. Major Australian cities and many towns hold these marches. Anzac Day is a public 
holiday. This reminds people that it is a very special day.
People lay flowers and wreaths at the base of war memorials to show that they respect 
and remember the men and women who served in the armed forces.
What is the Anzac spirit?
The Anzac spirit is the idea that the bravery and determination of the Australian and New 
Zealand soldiers lives on. The courage of the Anzacs will not be forgotten and people can 
try to be like them. The Anzac spirit is remembered in the Anzac Day motto: Lest we forget. 
The word lest in this motto means so we won’t.

Resource sheet – The Anzac spirit
Glorification or commemoration?
Hi, I’m Mitch. I don’t get this whole Anzac Day thing. 
Sure I like the public holiday but why are we glorifying 
war? We watch all these soldiers and their relatives 
march. If you ask me, we shouldn’t be remembering 
any wars. Think of all the innocent people who lost 
their lives. Think of all those young guys who were 
wounded for life. Think of all the places that were 
bombed. I reckon people are way too happy on Anzac 
Day. Heaps of them get drunk and some of them play 
that stupid two-up game. On the one hand, kids are 
told gambling is wrong, but it seems no one cares 
about it on Anzac Day. I think the whole Anzac Day 
thing is a myth.
Hi, I’m Libby. I attended the Dawn Service with my family this morning. Usually I hate 
getting up really early but for one special day of the year – Anzac Day – I don’t mind. 
After all, it’s a national day of commemoration when all Australians can remember 
the people who’ve fought for our country. Some of my friends think Anzac Day is a 
waste of time but they’ve forgotten that the courage of the Anzacs lives on today. 
It’s true that some veterans get drunk on Anzac Day but that’s probably because 
they’re trying to forget some of the horrors of war.  I know some of the veterans play 
that game, two-up, where they toss coins into the air. I don’t like gambling but I think 
that since soldiers played two-up in WWII, it’s ok for them to play it on Anzac Day. 
Even though I hate wars, Anzac Day is very special for me. I think everyone should 
respect those who’ve sacrificed so much for their country. The Anzac spirit should 
never be forgotten.

Anzac Day symbols 
A symbol is a representation (sign) of something. If you love someone, you might give 
them a red rose as a sign of your love. There are many symbols that help us remember the 
men and women who fought for Australia. These symbols are used in Anzac day Marches.
+ 
1	 Write each word beside the correct definition:  
bloodshed, bugle, rosemary, sacrifice, sprig, stirrups.
The giving up of something valuable or special to help 
a cause
Refers to people being killed in war
The metal or leather footrests that horse riders put 
their feet through
A brass musical instrument that looks like a small horn
A herb
A small branch of a plant
2	 Use these words to complete the information below: are, in, for, of, is.
• Many symbols _____ used in Anzac Day Marches. These symbols remind us _____ those 
who made great sacrifices in times _____ war _____ Australia and New Zealand.  
• The Anzac March _____ a symbol of a military funeral. On Anzac Day, a lot of people 
wear a sprig _____ rosemary because rosemary _____ a symbol of remembrance. 
Rosemary also grows on the Gallipoli peninsula. 
• Some people wear a red poppy because it _____ a symbol of sacrifice and bloodshed. 
• Two other symbols you can see on Anzac Day _____ the Rising Sun badge and the lone 
charger. The Rising Sun badge represents the Australian Army. The lone charger _____ a 
horse without a rider. The horse has a pair of reversed boots _____ its stirrups to remind 
people _____ soldiers who have lost their lives. 
• The Last Post _____ another symbol used on Anzac Day. It is a bugle call that _____ 
used to remember those who have lost their lives _____ war. Originally, the Last 
Post was used to signal the end of the day but now it _____ used to show that dead 
servicemen and servicewomen can rest _____ peace.

Resource sheet – The impact of settlement
Massacres 
Henry Mayrick and his brothers Alfred and Maurice were early settlers in the Western Port and 
Gippsland areas of Victoria. This source is part of a letter Henry wrote to his mother in April 1846. 
Definitions
wretches: victims, sufferers
unsparing perseverance:  
cruel persistence or determination
conceive: understand
penalty: price
familiarised: used to
participated: involved in 
remedy: change or fix
aloof: distant, detached
Source: H.H Mayrick, letters, 1840-1847, La Trobe Library,  
SLV H15789 – 15816
The blacks are very quiet here now, poor 
wretches, no wild beast of the forest was ever 
hunted down with such unsparing perseverance 
as they are; men, women and children are shot 
where ever they can be met with, some excuses 
might be found for shooting the men by those 
who are daily getting their cattle speared, but 
what they can urge in their excuse who shoot 
women and children I cannot conceive. I have 
protested against it at every station I have been 
in in Gipps [Gippsland] in the strongest language 
but these things are kept very secret as the 
penalty would be hanging … I remember the 
time when my blood would have run cold at 
the bare mention of these things but now I am 
become so familiarised with scenes of horror, 
from having murder made a topic of everyday 
conversation. I have heard tales told, and some 
things I have seen that would form as dark a page 
as ever you could read in the book of history  – 
but I thank God I have never participated in them 
– If I could remedy these things I would speak 
loudly though it cost me all I am worth in the 
world, but as I cannot I will keep aloof and know 
nothing and say nothing.

The role of a Protector
The  role of a ‘Pr _ t _ ct _ r of Aborigines’ 
was held by men in most states of 
A _ str _ l _ _ from the middle 1800s 
through to the early 1900s. The Protector 
was the legal guardian of Indigenous 
children to the age of 16 years. The 
Protector had the power to remove 
Ind _ g _ n _ _ s children from their family 
and place them in homes or in work. They 
also had control over who Indigenous 
adults could marry, where they could 
l _ ve, their h _ _ lth and their money. 
Aboriginals Protection and 
Restriction of the Sale of Opium 
Act 1897
This Act was created to pr _ t _ ct 
Indigenous people from disease 
and m _ str _ _ tm _ nt by the 
white community. But in practice, 
it meant that Indigenous people 
could be removed from their homes 
and placed in reserves. 
Dr Walter E Roth
Dr Roth was the ‘Northern Pr _ t _ ct _ r 
of Aborigines’ in Queensland. His job was 
to enforce the laws of the ‘Aboriginals 
Protection and R _ str _ ct _ _ n of the 
Sale of Op _ _ m Act of 1897’. Roth was 
well known for strongly applying the laws 
of the Act. 
The Industrial and Reformatory 
Schools Act 1865 (1865–1911) 
Queensland
This set of laws helped to set 
up special schools to educate 
children under the age of 15 who 
had broken the law or who were 
described as ‘neglected’. 
One way the Act defined a 
n _ gl _ ct _ d child was: “Any child 
born of an aboriginal or half-caste 
mother.” (7.)
Source: The acts of the Parliament of Queensland, 
Industrial and Reformatory Schools Act – 1865

Resource sheet – The Stolen Generation
Walter’s story
February 1903
Dr Walter E Roth was the Northern Protector of Aborigines, based in Cardwell, north Queensland. 
He wrote to D Graham, a Protector in Townsville:
Source 1
Sir, I have the honour to inform you that my attention has been drawn 
to the following h-c children roaming about the blacks’ camps in the 
neighbourhood of Cardwell . . . it seems to me a great pity to see the 
lad “Walter Peter” loaf ing around the camp instead of learning a trade 
at the Industrial School. 
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
June 8, 1903 
Dr Roth writes to the Under Secretary, Department of Public Lands:
Source 2
I would accordingly suggest that (1) “Walter” be 
brought up under the Industrial Schools Act of 
1865 . . . being a “child born of an aboriginal or 
half-caste mother.
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, 
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
August 1903
Fourteen-year-old Walter was charged with the offence of being neglected 
because he was a “child born of an aboriginal or half-caste mother”.
While locked up and waiting to be sent to an industrial school for two years, 
Walter became very ill from distress. His mother Nellie Bliss came to the lock-up. 
She howled and screamed in grief because her child was being taken away. 
Walter was released, but later tricked by Dr Roth into boarding a boat that took 
him away to Cairns. 
ISBN 978-0-6481150-8-3

© Blake Education 2020
Resource sheet – The Stolen Generation
A letter to Dr Roth
Source 3
November 27, 1903
In November a (iv) M. Matthews, Cardwell to Dr. Roth, Northern 
Protector of Aborigines, November 27, 1903.
Sir,
I would like to draw your attention to the way which “Walter” was 
kidnapped from here last Monday night – and sent away to Cairns to 
the Missionary Station. I presume the parents were informed by the 
police that he was to be let go on Tuesday morning but by that time he 
was well on his way to Cairns. He was coaxed to the steamer by telling 
him that the Inspector was on board and wanted to see him and he 
could go to his parents again on Tuesday morning. As I have known 
him since he was born, I know he had never been neglected in any 
way, was always well clothed and always had plenty to eat and now 
that he is over fifteen years of age and can earn “his own living” he is 
disgracefully taken away from his parents by the police.
His mother is crying after him and partly blames me for taking him to 
the boat. 
If other police left the blacks alone and looked after some of the 
neglected “whites” it would be much more to their credit as you know 
yourself the “blacks” here are not neglected and I consider it is about 
time it was put a stop to; even if Walter is a halfcaste why should he be 
kidnapped away from his parents. 
I would kindly ask you to give me a reply to this so as to know if there is 
any chance of his coming back to his parents.
I think it is one of the most disgraceful things that I have ever seen that 
the boy should be decoyed away from his parents in such a manner.
Trusting for a favourable reply,
I remain, Yours faithfully
M Matthews
Source: Queensland State Archives Item ID336387, (A/58751) Correspondence, Aboriginal and 
Torres Strait Islander

The cities of stinks
Source 1
Page xii 
SANITARY CONDITION OF 
ADELAIDE.  
Prior to the introduction of 
a system of deep drainage, 
Adelaide was drained partly by 
an imperfect system of sewers 
laid down by the corporation, 
and discharging in the park 
lands, and partly by open 
street-channels, by which the 
drainage ultimately found its 
way to the River Torrens. A 
few water-closets were in use 
connected with the corporation 
sewers, but cesspits were 
chiefly used, and their 
contents buried in the park 
lands. With this condition 
of things, Adelaide has been 
described by one witness as 
having been a “city of stinks”, 
with its subsoil surcharged 
with sewage. In 1885 a system 
of deep drainage was completed. 
The city is now free from 
offensive odours, the subsoil 
is recovering, the street 
channels are used only for 
surface water, and the Torrens 
has been changed from a f ilthy 
sewer to a beautiful hike. 
Source 2
Page xiii 
CONDITION OF SYDNEY. 
As early as 1854, underground 
sewers were laid down in 
the city of Sydney. These 
discharged directly into the 
harbour. Owing to complaints 
about the drainage and water 
supply and the pollution 
of the harbour, a board of 
inquiry was appointed in 
1875. As a result of their 
investigations, a complete 
system of deep drainage was 
commenced in 1880, and is now 
in course of construction. 
Main sewers have been laid 
down to intercept the drainage 
to the harbour, and to convey 
the sewage from the northern 
portion of the city by a large 
main sewer to the ocean at 
Bondi, where a strong current 
there prevailing carries away 
and disperses the discharged 
matters. 
. . . The southern portion of 
the city drains into a shallow 
estuary, and the sewage has 
been conducted by a main sewer 
to a sewage farm at Botany . . . 
Source: Sanitary condition, of Melbourne: Progress report of Royal Commission to inquire into and report upon the 
sanitary condition of Melbourne, presented to both Houses of Parliament by His Excellency’s command, 1889

Source: Easy stories for Australian children: a junior reader of Australian history correlated with geography, 
George Sutherland, 1900, pp. 14-16.
Lesson V.
THE TASMANIAN BLACKS.
	
The Tasmanian blacks were not nearly so tall as the 
sailors of Tasman thought them to be. Indeed, they were 
shorter than the Australian blacks, and belonged to a 
different race, not unlike the negroes, having curly or 
frizzly hair, and a shiny, black skin.
	
Black people of the same kind are still to be found on 
islands of the Indian and Pacif ic Oceans, mostly hiding 
away in dark parts of the forests. The Tasmanian blacks 
were also very shy, and would not make friends with the 
whites.
	
After the white people went to settle in Tasmania they 
often tried to be friendly with the blacks. Governor Davey 
got a friend to draw a picture showing that the whites 
ought to be kind to the blacks, and the blacks ought not 
to kill the whites. This was printed, and copies of it were 
stuck on the trees for the blacks to see.
	
Yet still the f ighting went on. Tribes of blacks hiding 
in the bush would come out now and then, and kill some 
lonely settler; and then the whites would take their guns, 
and kill as many blacks as they could f ind. A long line 
of riflemen tried to drive all the blacks into a corner of 
the island, but only one was caught.
	
At last a settler named Robinson began to search for 
the blacks in a friendly way, and, after f ive years of 
very dangerous work in tracking them through the bush, 
he collected them together. Houses were built for them 
on South Bruni Island, and in other places, where they 
were kindly treated. Yet they all died off. The last black 
woman lived till 1876.

1	 Gill included fun stick figures in many of his advertisements. Circle them, and any other unusual 
or funny parts of the image. Why are they included?
	
	
	
	
	
	
2	 Highlight the part of the image that shows Indigenous people. What does this image suggest 
about Indigenous people living in the Melbourne area at this time?
	
	
	
	
	
	
3	 Highlight another part of the image that stands out to you. Why did you choose this part? 
	
	
	
	
	
	
4	 What does the whole image suggest to you about the environment around Melbourne and life 
at this time?
	
	
	
	
	
	
5	 According to the words in the advertisement, what subjects does Gill show in his lithographs? 
	
	
	
	
6	 Why would people living in Melbourne want images of these subjects? What would they do with 
the images?
